sudan.title: «الخماسية»قلقة من تصاعد هجمات المسيّرات في السودان وتدعو لهدنة إنسانية - سودان تربيون
sudan.summary: أعربت الآلية الخماسية، التي تضم الأمم المتحدة والاتحاد الأفريقي ومنظمة إيقاد والجامعة العربية والاتحاد الأوروبي، عن قلقها المتزايد بشأن تصاعد هجمات الطائرات المسيّرة في السودان، محذرة من تأثيراتها السلبية على المدنيين والبنية التحتية. في بيانها، أدانت الآلية الهجمات التي استهدفت عدة ولايات، بما في ذلك الخرطوم ودارفور، مما أسفر عن سقوط ضحايا مدنيين وتدمير مرافق حيوية مثل محطات الكهرباء والمرافق الصحية. وأشارت إلى أن هذه الأضرار أدت إلى انقطاع واسع للتيار الكهربائي وتعطيل الخدمات الأساسية، مما زاد من تفاقم الأوضاع الإنسانية. ودعت الآلية إلى وقف فوري للأعمال العدائية وحماية المدنيين، مؤكدة أنه لا يوجد حل عسكري للأزمة. كما أكدت على أهمية الالتزام بالقانون الدولي الإنساني وضرورة العودة إلى مسار سياسي شامل يقوده السودانيون، مشددة على أهمية جهود خفض التصعيد.

الجوع ويعمل عشرات الشباب في التكايا -أرشيفية الخرطوم 14 نوفمبر 2026 – تشهد البنية الاجتماعية والاقتصادية في السودان تآكلاً غير مسبوق في شبكات الأمان التكافلية والمنظومات الحكومية للحماية الاجتماعية، إثر التداعيات المتواصلة للنزاع المسلح المتطاول. وأدى الصراع المستمر بين الجيش السوداني وقوات الدعم السريع، إلى تدمير أدوات المواجهة المعيشية الأساسية للأسرة السودانية وشبكات الأمان الاجتماعي والجمعيات التي كانت في الأحياء. ومع خروج المؤسسات الخدمية عن السيطرة وانقطاع سبل الكسب، تحولت شبكات الأمان التكافلية التقليدية مثل “النفير” و”التكايا” والروابط الأسرية الرافدة للمساعدات إلى حالة من الإنهاك الكلي، مما رفع معدلات الفقر إلى مستويات قياسية وألقى بالملايين في مواجهة مكشوفة مع عواصف انعدام الأمن الغذائي والنزوح القسري. أنماط الانهيار يرى عضو غرفة الطوارئ، عبد الرحمن درملي، أن أكثر أنماط الفقر بروزًا إثر انهيار شبكات الأمان الاجتماعي تمثلت في طبقة الموظفين، بعد فقدانهم سبل مواجهة متطلبات السوق وتغطية تكاليف المعيشة. وأوضح درملي، في حديث لـ”سودان تربيون”، أن العمالة الماهرة واجهت بدورها ظروفًا معقدة، غير أن بعض المجموعات تمكنت من تجاوزها عبر نقل خبراتها إلى الولايات ومناطق النزوح. وأشار إلى وجود تفاوت في مستويات التكافل تجاه النازحين؛ إذ أبدت مجتمعات استمرارًا في تقديم الدعم، مقابل مجتمعات أخرى قدمت ما بوسعها سابقًا وتوقف دعمها جراء تدهور الأوضاع الاقتصادية، بينما انتقد مجموعات ثالثة اتسمت بالموقف السلبي ولم تقدم أي مساهمة في تعزيز الشبكات الاجتماعية. ولفت درملي إلى مهددات تحيط بشبكات الأمان الاجتماعي والتكافل، وفي مقدمتها غياب الأمن والاستقرار والعدالة. في المقابل، أكد وجود دور لافت لفاعلين في إسناد شبكات التكافل التقليدية، وفي مقدمتهم التجار المحليون الذين يتحملون مخاطر عالية لنقل المواد الغذائية إلى المناطق الخطرة، وينسقون جهودًا لمواجهة المجاعة واستمرار عمل المطابخ الجماعية. وجزم أنه رغم قسوة الظروف الحالية، فإن هناك أطرافًا عديدة تنشط في حماية شبكات الأمان الاجتماعي والدفاع عنها. فراغ رقمي ولم تقتصر الأزمة على تجميد البرامج الحكومية المباشرة كصندوق الدعم الاجتماعي والمساعدات الموجهة للشرائح الضعيفة فحسب، بل امتدت لتطال البنية التحتية المعلوماتية وتدمير السجلات الرقمية للرعاية والتكافل، مما أحدث فراغاً تشريعياً وميدانياً عجزت المبادرات المحلية والإغاثية عن سده بالكامل في ظل التضخم المتصاعد وانهيار قيمة العملة الوطنية. وقالت مصادر في وزارة المالية لـ”سودان تربيون” إن الوزارة لم تقم بصرف أي أموال للدعم الاجتماعي أو شبكاته خلال هذا العام، بخلاف بعض الأموال التي يصدقها الوزير لبعض النشاطات المرتبطة بمجموعات رفضت تسميتها. وفي موازنة عام 2026 الطارئة التي أجازها مجلس الوزراء السوداني برئاسة وزارة المالية، لم تُعلن الحكومة نسبة مئوية مخصصة ومحددة بشكل تفصيلي للدعم الاجتماعي من إجمالي الموازنة ضمن منشوراتها الرسمية أو مؤتمراتها الصحفية. وذكرت المصادر أن الموازنة تضمنت زيادة الحد الأدنى للمعاش الشهري ليصل إلى نحو 450 ألف جنيه سوداني كدعم اجتماعي مباشر وفقاً للمصادر، مضيفة أن الموازنة ركزت اعتمادات الإنفاق المالي في موازنة 2026 بشكل أساسي على المجهود الحربي، وتوفير الخدمات الأساسية الطارئة. تقليص خطير وأكد مفوض مفوضية الأمان الاجتماعي والتكافل وخفض الفقر، الدكتور محمد علي سالم، خلال اجتماعه مع المعهد الدولي لبحوث السياسات الغذائية (IFPRI) في 24 أغسطس 2026، أن استمرار النزاع أحدث تقليصاً خطيراً في فاعلية التدخلات الموجهة للفئات الأكثر احتياجاً. وقال إن المفوضية تسعى لتعزيز الشراكات المؤسسية والبحثية لإعادة بناء قاعدة البيانات المفقودة، ودعم منظومة الحماية الاجتماعية بناءً على الأدلة والبيانات الحقلية لتفادي التداعي الكامل للبنية التكافلية في السودان. من جانبه، صرح وزير التنمية الاجتماعية، في نوفمبر 2025، مبيناً الأثر المباشر للنزاع على المؤشرات الاقتصادية الاجتماعية بأن معدل الفقر في البلاد شهد قفزة كارثية حيث ارتفع من 21% ليصل إلى نحو 71% نتيجة تراجع إيرادات الدولة، وزيادة الإنفاق الموجه لمواجهة متطلبات الحرب، وتوقف معظم الأنشطة الإنتاجية التي كانت تشكل مظلة الدعم للشرائح الفقيرة. انحسار المساعدات وحذرت المديرة العامة للمنظمة الدولية للهجرة، آمي بوب، في بيان رسمي حول الاستجابة الإنسانية في السودان الصادر في سبتمبر 2026، من الشلل الوشيك لشرايين الدعم الأساسية. وقالت إن توقف الدعم السياسي والمالي بات يهدد عمل أكثر من 100 منظمة إغاثية، ويعطل الوصول إلى الملايين في المناطق الأكثر تضرراً. وفي تصريح مشترك صادر عن الوكالات الأممية الأربع (الهجرة الدولية، مفوضية اللاجئين، اليونيسف، وبرنامج الأغذية العالمي) في نيويورك في 24 أكتوبر 2025، تحدث نائب المدير العام للعمليات بالمنظمة الدولية للهجرة، أوغوتشي دانيلز، عن عمق تآكل شبكات الإيواء المحلية، وقال: “التقينا بعائلات عادت إلى مدن مدمّرة بالكامل، بلا ماء ولا كهرباء، حيث المستشفيات متوقفة والمدارس مغلقة، ومع ذلك تحاول هذه الأسر إعادة بناء حياتها من الصفر. إن أكثر من 900 يوم من القتال وتداعي الخدمات الحيوية دفعت أكثر من 30 مليون سوداني إلى حافة البقاء على قيد الحياة، وسط انهيار كامل لأجهزة الحماية الاجتماعية والشبكات الأهلية المستنزفة”. سودانية، اليوم السبت، عن مقتل عشرة مدنيين جراء إطلاق نار من قبل عناصر تابعة لقوات الدعم السريع في مدينة النهود. وتعد هذه المدينة المركز التجاري الثاني والأهم في ولاية غرب كردفان، حيث تشهد تصعيداً ميدانياً خطيراً خلال الساعات الأخيرة. وأكدت هيئة طوارئ دار حمر في بيان رسمي أن المدينة تعاني من حالة فوضى عارمة وانفلات أمني غير مسبوق. وأوضحت الهيئة أن انتهاكات واسعة تُرتكب بحق السكان من قبل عناصر تستقل دراجات نارية وتجوب الأحياء السكنية مسببة حالة من الذعر العام. وتعتبر منطقة دار حمر التي تقع فيها مدينة النهود من المناطق الجغرافية والقبلية الاستراتيجية في ولاية غرب كردفان. وتعد النهود الحاضرة الرئيسية لهذه المنطقة، مما يجعل استقرارها أمراً حيوياً للتوازن الاجتماعي والاقتصادي في الإقليم. وأشار البيان الصادر عن الهيئة إلى أن عمليات الاغتيال طالت 10 مواطنين عزل في أحياء متفرقة من المدينة منذ يوم الخميس الماضي. وتزامنت هذه الجرائم مع انقطاع كامل لخدمات الاتصالات والإنترنت الفضائي (ستارلينك) في المنطقة، مما عزل السكان عن العالم الخارجي. وأفادت مصادر محلية بأن عمليات نهب واسعة النطاق استهدفت المتاجر والأسواق الرئيسية في قلب المدينة. كما تعرضت منازل المواطنين لاقتحامات متكررة من قبل المسلحين، الذين قاموا بترويع العائلات والاستيلاء على ممتلكاتهم تحت تهديد السلاح. تأتي هذه التطورات الميدانية المتسارعة في ظل تقدم ملحوظ للجيش السوداني في محاور ولاية غرب كردفان. حيث تمكنت القوات المسلحة من بسط سيطرتها على مدينة الخوي يوم الجمعة، وهي مدينة استراتيجية تبعد نحو 100 كيلومتر عن مدينة النهود. وكان مسؤولون سودانيون قد أعلنوا في وقت سابق عن نجاح الجيش والقوات المساندة له في استعادة مدينة الخوي بعد معارك ضارية. وانسحبت قوات الدعم السريع من المنطقة عقب اشتباكات عنيفة أدت إلى تغيير في خارطة السيطرة sudan.summary: أعلنت لجنة الأمل للعودة الطوعية السودانية عن عودة 735 شخصًا من مصر إلى السودان عبر 15 حافلة، في إطار برنامج العودة الطوعية. تم نقل هؤلاء السودانيين من منطقة المطبعة في الجيزة، حيث أبدت اللجنة استعدادها لاستيعاب المزيد من الراغبين في العودة. وقد أشار رئيس اللجنة، محمد وداعة، إلى وجود رغبة من جهات دولية للمساهمة في إعادة السودانيين إلى وطنهم، داعيًا الراغبين في العودة إلى تحديث بياناتهم عبر رابط إلكتروني خاص. منذ بداية النزاع في السودان في أبريل 2023، فر أكثر من 1.2 مليون سوداني إلى مصر، حيث كان يقيم حوالي 5 ملايين سوداني قبل الحرب. حتى الآن، عاد نحو 428 ألف شخص طوعًا إلى السودان، في إطار مبادرة أطلقتها السلطات المصرية لتسهيل العودة. يهدف البرنامج إلى تسهيل عودة المواطنين السودانيين بشكل اختياري ومجاني.

sudan.summary: أعلنت المفوضية الوطنية للانتخابات في جنوب السودان عن تأجيل الانتخابات العامة إلى 11 فبراير 2027، بدلاً من الموعد السابق المحدد في 22 ديسمبر 2026. يتضمن الجدول الزمني الجديد بدء تسجيل الناخبين يدوياً في 14 نوفمبر 2026، والذي سيستمر حتى 28 من نفس الشهر. بعد ذلك، سيتم نشر سجل الناخبين الأولي. ستبدأ فترة تقديم طلبات الترشح في 14 ديسمبر وتستمر حتى 20 من الشهر ذاته، مع نشر القائمة النهائية للمرشحين بين 18 و21 يناير 2027. الحملة الانتخابية ستبدأ في 27 ديسمبر 2026 وتستمر لمدة 45 يوماً، على أن يتم إعلان النتائج النهائية في 17 فبراير 2027. تأتي هذه الانتخابات بعد تأجيلات متعددة بسبب التحديات السياسية والأمنية، وهي الأولى منذ استقلال جنوب السودان في 2011.

sudan.content: الانتقال إلى المحتوى الرئيسي Reporting the Changing World وكالتنا لمحة عن تاريخ الوكالة التوصيف الوظيفي نظام إدارة الجودة مبادئ-النشر السياسات-الخاصة-بالإعلام-الاجتماعي سياسة الخصوصية والكوكيز سياسة الإفصاح RSS التواصل بيانات الاتصال طلبات الاشتراك Anadolu Ajansı © 2026 تركيا الدول العربية دولي اقتصاد رياضة تقارير السودان.. مقتل 10 مدنيين برصاص "الدعم السريع" في مدينة النهود كوب 31 أنطاليا 3 سنوات من الإبادة الاعتداءات في الضفة الغربية EDITION Türkçe English BHSC Pусский Français العربية Kurdî کوردی Shqip فارسی македонски Bahasa Indonesia Español السودان السودان.. مقتل 10 مدنيين برصاص "الدعم السريع" في مدينة النهود منذ الخميس الماضي، وسط عمليات نهب واسعة واقتحام منازل المواطنين وترويعهم، وفق هيئة طوارئ دار حمر، دون تعليق من قوات الدعم السريع.. Adel Abdelrheem 14 نوفمبر 2026 • تحديث : 14 نوفمبر 2026 الأرشيف SUDAN عادل عبد الرحيم/ الأناضول أعلنت هيئة إغاثة سودانية، السبت، مقتل 10 مدنيين على يد قوات الدعم السريع في مدينة النهود، ثاني أكبر مدن ولاية غرب كردفان. وأفادت هيئة طوارئ دار حمر، في بيان، بأن مدينة النهود تشهد فوضى عارمة وانفلاتًا أمنيًا جراء انتهاكات تنفذها قوات الدعم السريع على متن دراجات نارية. و"دار حمر" منطقة جغرافية وقبلية معروفة في ولاية غرب كردفان، والنهود هي مركزها الرئيسي. وأضاف البيان: "قامت عناصر الدعم السريع باغتيال 10 مواطنين عزل في أحياء متفرقة بالمدينة منذ يوم الخميس الماضي، بالتزامن مع إغلاق كامل لجميع شبكات الاتصالات (ستارلينك)، فيما تتواصل حتى اللحظة عمليات نهب واسعة للمتاجر واقتحام منازل المواطنين وترويعهم". ولم يصدر تعليق فوري من قوات الدعم السريع، التي تسيطر على مدينة النهود منذ مايو/ أيار 2025. وتأتي هذه التطورات بالتزامن مع تقدم الجيش في ولاية غرب كردفان، عقب سيطرته على مدينة الخوي، الجمعة، التي تبعد نحو 100 كيلومتر عن مدينة النهود بولاية غرب كردفان. والجمعة، سيطر الجيش السوداني والقوات المساندة له على مدينة الخوي بولاية غرب كردفان جنوبي البلاد، بعد معارك مع قوات الدعم السريع، وفق إعلان مسؤولين سودانيين. والسبت الماضي، سيطر الجيش على منطقة "عيال بخيت" شمال غربي مدينة الخوي، بعد معارك مع قوات الدعم السريع، وفق مصادر مطلعة للأناضول. وتأتي هذه التطورات في ظل تصاعد المواجهات العسكرية بين الجيش وقوات الدعم السريع في ولايات إقليم كردفان الثلاث، شمال وغرب وجنوب، منذ 25 أكتوبر/ تشرين الأول الماضي. ومنذ أبريل/ نيسان 2023، يشهد السودان حربًا بين الجيش وقوات الدعم السريع، أسفرت عن مقتل عشرات الآلاف ونزوح نحو 13 مليون شخص، وفق تقديرات أممية. news_share news_share_description وفي ظل الظروف الاقتصادية والاجتماعية الصعبة التي تعيشها أسر كثيرة، وما خلفته الحرب والنزوح من تحولات عميقة في حياة المجتمع، وجد أطفال أنفسهم أمام أدوار لم تكن مناسبة لأعمارهم؛ بعضهم اضطر إلى العمل المنزل، ثم يخرج بحثاً عن عمل يساعد به أسرته، قبل أن يعود في نهاية اليوم مرهقاً، حاملاً في ذهنه حسابات المعيشة. يقول مجاهد البالغ من العمر 14 عاماً لـ”سودان تربيون” : كنت أحلم مثل كل الأطفال لأكون مهندساً وأقضي وقتي مع أصحابي، لكن الظروف جعلتني أفكر كيف أساعد أسرتي. أم صغيرة أما نعمات، البالغة من العمر 13 عاماً، فقد وجدت نفسها أمام مسؤوليات منزلية متزايدة بعد أن أصبحت والدتها تتحمل أعباء إعالة الأسرة وحدها. تقول نعمات لـ”سودان تربيون” : “أستيقظ مبكراً لتجهيز إخوتي وأساعد في البيت، وأحياناً ليس لدي وقت لمراجعة دروسي. وتابعت: أتمنى أن أعود كما السابق ألعب من غير تفكير في تجهيز حاجات المنزل. “ وتضيف أن أكثر ما تفتقده هو الوقت الذي كانت تقضيه مع صديقاتها، وأنها تحلم بالعودة إلى الدراسة ومواصلة تعليمها. وتكشف حالة نعمات جانباً آخر من الطفولة المؤجلة، يتمثل في الأعباء المنزلية والرعاية غير المدفوعة التي تتحملها بعض الفتيات في سن مبكرة، وهي مسؤوليات قد تؤثر على تعليمهن وراحتهن النفسية وفرص نموهن الطبيعي. أحلام توقفت عند أبواب النزوح أما علي البالغ من العمر 15 عاماً، فلم يضع في حسبانه أن تتغير حياته بهذه السرعة. كان طالباً يحب المدرسة ويحلم بمواصلة تعليمه، لكن النزوح وما صاحبه من اضطراب في حياة أسرته جعلا استمراره في الدراسة أمراً بالغ الصعوبة. ويقول لـ”سودان تربيون” : “ أكثر حاجة آلمته ابتعاده عن المدرسة والأصدقاء. فحلمه كان إكمال تعليمه، لكن بات تفكيره منشغلاً بتوفير المسكن والأكل والاحتياجات الأساسية. “ وبين محاولات الأسرة التكيف مع واقعها الجديد، يجد علي نفسه أمام مستقبل بلا معالم، تتراجع فيه أحلامه التعليمية أمام الأولويات اليومية. وتوضح قصته أن آثار النزوح لا تتوقف عند فقدان المنزل أو تغيير مكان الإقامة، بل تمتد إلى المسار التعليمي والاجتماعي للأطفال، وقد تترك فجوات يصعب تجاوزها دون تدخل ودعم مناسبين. طفولة خلف أبواب المستشفيات وفي جانب آخر من المعاناة، تعيش مريم، البالغة من العمر 12 عاماً، تجربة مختلفة؛ إذ تقضي وقتاً طويلاً في مرافقة والدتها المريضة ومساعدتها في بعض شؤون المنزل، إلى جانب اهتمامها بإخوتها الصغار. تقول مريم لـ”سودان تربيون” إنها تحب والدتها ولا تستطيع تركها بمفردها، لكن تشعر في بعض الأحيان بالتعب والاشتياق إلى اللعب والذهاب للمدرسة مثل بقية الأطفال. وتابعت: “ أتمنى أن تتعافى أمي ونعود لحياتنا العادية”. أطفال في أوضاع خطرة يؤكد الأمين العام للمجلس القومي لرعاية الطفولة، عبدالقادر أبو، أن نحو 71% من أطفال السودان يعيشون في وضع خطر نتيجة للانتهاكات والتداعيات الإنسانية والأمنية المرتبطة بالحرب. وأوضح عبدالقادر أبو لـ”سودان تربيون” أن هناك ما بين 11 إلى 12 ولاية سودانية تُصنف كولايات آمنة بنسبة أمان تتجاوز 85%. إلا أن ممارسات واعتداءات الدعم السريع وأعوانها أدت إلى تضرر عدد من المدارس، فضلاً عن تفاقم ظلال الفقر وظلماته على الأسر السودانية. وقال إن أعمال الإحصاء والملاحقة الديموغرافية في المجلس أظهرت أن ما بين 60% إلى 65% من الأطفال في سن التمدرس هم خارج المدارس حالياً. ويعمل هؤلاء الأطفال كمساعدين في حافلات النقل العام والباصات، وفي التعدين الأهلي، إضافة إلى العمل في المطاعم والأسواق. وأشار أبو إلى أن الانتهاكات الجسيمة التي سببتها ميليشيا الدعم السريع انعكست سلباً وبشكل مباشر على حياة وسلامة أطفال السودان، وأضاف أن المجلس يعمل بالتعاون مع منظمات المجتمع المدني الوطنية ووكالات الأمم المتحدة في الولايات الآمنة على تحويل November 14, 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp Linkedin Telegram Viber The author (File Photo) Girma Berhanu (Professor) Ethiopia’s Crisis and the Paradox of Civil Resistance: Where Is the Collective Outrage? Ethiopia is confronting a profound national crisis characterised by widespread poverty, devastating armed conflicts, mass displacement, political repression, economic deterioration, and the destruction of communities and livelihoods. Millions of families have experienced the loss of loved ones; millions have been displaced; and countless citizens struggle to survive amid uncertainty, insecurity, and despair. The country’s social fabric is increasingly fractured, while the institutions entrusted with protecting citizens often appear incapable of guaranteeing their security, dignity, and fundamental rights. Yet, amid this extraordinary suffering, one question continues to haunt the Ethiopian political landscape: Why has civil resistance not emerged with the breadth, intensity, and national coherence that the magnitude of the crisis would seem to demand? This is not a question intended to blame victims of repression or to underestimate the courage of those who have resisted injustice. Ethiopia has witnessed remarkable acts of resistance, protest, and political courage. Nevertheless, the persistence and scale of the national crisis raise serious questions about the structural, political, social, and psychological barriers that impede the emergence of sustained, inclusive, and transformative civil resistance. A Personal Reflection: The Politics of Youth Mobilisation I sometimes reflect on my own political experiences during my youth. At the time, I was responsible for an underground movement within the Youth Vanguard section of the Ethiopian People’s Revolutionary Party (EPRP). I probably had around 200 young people under my command, some of whom were organised into what were referred to as urban guerrilla active groups. Many of these young people were between 12 and 15 years old. What remains particularly striking in my memory is the extraordinary level of passion, commitment, and political engagement among these young people. Their dedication was remarkable. They were prepared, quite literally, to risk their lives in carrying out the movement’s directives. We were engaged in clandestine and subversive activities, although not in armed struggle. We wanted action—real action. There was an almost overwhelming determination to challenge and overthrow the military junta, which we regarded as a fascist regime. Of course, we were children. We did not fully understand the political, ideological, and historical complexities of the struggle in which we were involved. We were deeply influenced by the revolutionary ideology and political environment of the time, and, in many respects, profoundly indoctrinated. Our activities were also constrained by the circumstances surrounding the gradual disintegration of the EPRP itself. Looking back, I am struck by the intensity of our political consciousness, collective commitment, and willingness to engage in resistance, even under extremely dangerous circumstances. This is not to romanticize our involvement or the recruitment of children into clandestine political activities. Rather, it is to reflect on the extraordinary capacity of young people to become politically mobilized, particularly when they believe that their society is facing an existential crisis. This personal recollection inevitably leads me to a difficult and uncomfortable question: What explains the apparent political passivity of significant sections of the younger generation in Ethiopia today, despite the extraordinary levels of suffering, deprivation, subjugation, violence, and injustice surrounding them? People are starving. Communities are being destroyed. Homes are demolished, sometimes with devastating consequences for entire families. Ethnic hatred and political violence have become deeply embedded in everyday life. Consider, for example, the heartbreaking account of a child reportedly eaten by hyenas while the child’s single mother had gone back to retrieve whatever belongings she could salvage following the demolition of their home. Such accounts are almost impossible to comprehend, yet they illustrate the extreme vulnerability and human suffering experienced by ordinary citizens. How should we understand the apparent absence of a broad-based, sustained, and coordinated collective response to such conditions? Perhaps the comparison between my generation and today’s youth is not entirely fair. The political, social, technological, and institutional contexts are fundamentally different. Moreover, what appears to be passivity may, in fact, conceal fear, exhaustion, fragmentation, political disillusionment, or forms of resistance that are less visible and less organised. Decades of authoritarian rule, surveillance, repression, ethnic polarisation, and the fragmentation of political opposition may have profoundly weakened the possibilities for collective mobilisation. Nevertheless, the question remains important. Understanding this paradox requires us to look beyond individual courage or the apparent absence of political will. We must examine the structural conditions that shape collective action: the erosion of trust, the fragmentation of social identities, the absence of credible political leadership, the costs of resistance, and the psychological consequences of prolonged exposure to violence and insecurity. Understanding this paradox is essential not only for confronting Ethiopia’s present crisis but also for imagining a different political future—one in which citizens can reclaim their agency, dignity, and collective capacity to shape the society in which they live. Resilience, Dignity, and the Possibility of Rising Again In reflecting on resistance, I am reminded of the words and political legacy of Stokely Carmichael (Kwame Ture), the African American civil rights activist and prominent Black Power leader. His reflections on the limitations of nonviolence under conditions of oppression raise difficult questions about the relationship between resistance, power, and the conscience of those who exercise it. I am also reminded of Maya Angelou’s celebrated poem Still I Rise . Its message of resilience, dignity, and defiance in the face of oppression speaks powerfully to societies and individuals subjected to humiliation, hatred, injustice, and suffering. Angelou’s poem reminds us that adversity does not have to define the human spirit. Lies, hatred, and humiliation may inflict profound wounds, but they need not determine one’s worth or future. To rise is to reclaim one’s dignity, confidence, freedom, and hope. It is to refuse to allow oppression and suffering to have the final word. For Ethiopia, this message has particular significance. The challenge is not simply to endure suffering or demonstrate individual resilience. It is to transform individual experiences of injustice and despair into a shared commitment to human dignity, solidarity, justice, and a more inclusive political future. Ultimately, the question is not merely why people are not resisting more visibly. It is also what political, social, and psychological conditions would make collective resistance possible, sustainable, and transformative . How can a deeply fragmented and traumatised society recover its collective agency and rediscover the courage to imagine and struggle for a different future? The Paradox of Suffering Without Collective Transformation Political history repeatedly demonstrates that widespread suffering does not automatically translate into collective resistance. Poverty, oppression, and political exclusion may generate anger and resentment, but anger alone does not create a movement capable of transforming political power. Civil resistance requires something more: collective consciousness, organizational capacity, political trust, strategic coordination, shared objectives, and a belief that meaningful change is possible. In Ethiopia, these conditions have been repeatedly undermined by repression, political fragmentation, ethnic polarization, economic vulnerability, and the historical predominance of armed struggle. Consequently, national suffering has often produced fragmented resistance rather than a unified movement capable of confronting the underlying structures of political injustice. The tragedy is that a society experiencing extraordinary collective hardship may remain politically divided precisely when unity becomes most necessary. Fear as an Instrument of Political Control One of the most powerful explanations for the limited scale of sustained civil resistance is the pervasive climate of fear. In contexts where political dissent can expose individuals to arrest, imprisonment, intimidation, violence, or even death, resistance becomes an extraordinarily risky personal and collective undertaking. When I have asked people in Ethiopia why they do not resist their suffering and the injustices they experience, a recurring response has been fear of retaliation—not only against themselves but also against their relatives and next of kin. Many fear that the consequences of political opposition could extend to their families, making the personal cost of resistance almost unbearable. Through such practices, the regime has succeeded in cultivating a climate of deep-seated fear and political intimidation among citizens. This climate of fear also extends into the Ethiopian diaspora. Even abroad, many people remain reluctant to express open opposition to the regime. Some are primarily concerned with protecting their personal interests, maintaining access to their homeland, and being able to visit relatives without attracting unwanted attention or interrogation from the authorities. In my observation, this has become one of the dividing lines within the diaspora: between those willing to speak out despite the potential consequences and those who choose silence, caution, or accommodation. This division reflects not only the effectiveness of political intimidation but also a deeper problem of political opportunism and self-preservation that has become embedded in aspects of our social and political culture. What is particularly troubling is that fear can persist even in relatively free societies, where individuals theoretically enjoy the freedom to condemn human rights violations and political atrocities. Fear is often amplified through propaganda, intimidation, surveillance, and deliberate narratives about the consequences of dissent. The regime actively cultivates and reproduces this atmosphere, extending its influence beyond national borders. The result is a disturbing situation in which political resistance becomes increasingly fragmented, muted, and, in some instances, almost invisible—even among communities living outside the country. My own position has always been grounded in the principle that injustice and political oppression must be confronted before they become irreversible. I strongly believe in the necessity of resisting tyranny rather than passively waiting for its destructive consequences. This does not mean embracing violence or retaliation; rather, it means refusing to surrender the moral, political, and civic space to those who govern through intimidation and fear. Political courage, solidarity, and collective action are essential if a society is to reclaim its dignity and freedom. Fear does not necessarily eliminate political opposition. Instead, it can prevent opposition from becoming visible, coordinated, and sustained. Citizens may privately reject political repression while publicly remaining silent. Communities may recognize injustice while lacking the security or organizational capacity to challenge it. Individuals may desire political transformation but hesitate because the consequences of participation could extend to their families, livelihoods, and communities. This is precisely how repression undermines collective action: not necessarily by convincing people that injustice is acceptable, but by making resistance appear prohibitively dangerous. Therefore, the absence of mass mobilization should not be confused with public consent. Silence under repression is not necessarily consent; it may be the expression of a society living under the calculated consequences of fear. Fragmented National Identity and the Crisis of Solidarity Perhaps one of the most consequential obstacles to sustained civil resistance in Ethiopia is the fragmentation of political identity and national solidarity. Ethnic federalism, historical grievances, competing nationalist narratives, and unresolved questions of political power and territorial belonging have contributed to deep divisions within Ethiopian society. These divisions increasingly shape how citizens interpret political violence, injustice, and human suffering. The suffering of one community may attract widespread attention, while that of another is minimized, justified, or dismissed. Political allegiance can take precedence over the fundamental principle that all civilian lives deserve equal protection. The recurring massacres of civilians and worshippers in Arsi Zone, Oromia, which have reportedly intensified in recent weeks, illustrate this troubling pattern. More broadly, the suffering of the Amhara population has often been marginalized, underreported, or silenced. In some instances, victims are even blamed for the violence perpetrated against them. I find particularly distressing the apparent silence of significant sections of the Oromo community in response to the atrocities in Arsi. The absence of stronger public condemnation and cross-community solidarity raises serious questions about the erosion of a shared moral responsibility. Such selective empathy undermines the ethical foundations of a genuinely national movement. Civil resistance cannot become transformative if it mobilizes people exclusively around the grievances of one ethnic group, region, or political constituency while disregarding the rights and suffering of others. Nor can national solidarity be built on selective recognition of victims or the politicization of human suffering. The central challenge, therefore, is not simply to organize resistance against a particular government or political leadership. It is to cultivate a shared commitment to equal citizenship and the principle that no Ethiopian should be subjected to violence, discrimination, or political exclusion because of their identity. Without such solidarity, collective resistance risks reproducing the very divisions and exclusions that sustain political instability. A genuinely national struggle for freedom must recognize the suffering of all communities, reject selective compassion, and defend the dignity and rights of every citizen without exception. A Crisis of Political Leadership and Organizational Credibility Civil resistance does not emerge spontaneously from public suffering. It requires credible leadership and organizational structures capable of transforming individual grievances into collective political action. Civil resistance is a long-standing and widespread phenomenon in human history. Several works on civil resistance adopt a historical approach to the analysis of the subject.Cases of civil resistance, both successful and unsuccessful, include tens. My observation is that those which suceed had a great organisational skills and strong political leadership. Ethiopian opposition movements have frequently been weakened by ideological disagreements, personal rivalries, organizational fragmentation, competing political mbitions, and insufficient coordination. In some instances, political organizations have struggled to articulate a vision that transcends ethnic and regional constituencies. This fragmentation has contributed to public skepticism about whether existing political actors can genuinely deliver democratic transformation. Citizens may oppose the prevailing political order without necessarily trusting those who claim to represent its alternatives. The resulting crisis of credibility is particularly damaging because successful civil resistance requires confidence that participation serves a meaningful collective purpose. Civil Resistance: An Alternative to Endless Destruction Civil resistance offers Ethiopia an important possibility: achieving political transformation through organized, collective, and nonviolent action rather than perpetuating cycles of armed confrontation and destruction. Nonviolent resistance is neither passive nor politically insignificant. It can challenge the legitimacy of oppressive institutions, mobilize public participation, expose injustice, and generate pressure for meaningful political change. Its strength lies in the ability of ordinary citizens to withdraw their cooperation from unjust systems and collectively assert their political agency. In the long run, I see little prospect of sustainable political transformation in Ethiopia without well-organized civil resistance, a coherent political vision, and an inclusive strategy for implementation. Ethiopia’s transition from the Tigrayan-dominated EPRDF leadership to the Prosperity Party illustrates how political change can emerge from the interaction of internal power struggles and mass popular mobilization. However, leadership changes alone do not necessarily produce democratic transformation or dismantle authoritarian structures. Civil resistance should not, however, be romanticized as an automatic solution. Its effectiveness depends on organizational capacity, strategic discipline, broad public participation, solidarity across social divisions, and the ability to sustain collective action despite repression. It also requires a clear political vision of what should follow the transformation of the existing order. A movement that mobilizes against injustice but fails to establish credible democratic alternatives risks reproducing the same patterns of exclusion, political domination, and authoritarianism. The objective, therefore, must be more ambitious than simply replacing political leaders. It must be to fundamentally transform the relationship between political power and the people, establishing accountable institutions, equal citizenship, democratic participation, and respect for human rights. Conclusion Ethiopia is experiencing a profound national catastrophe marked by armed conflict, mass displacement, political repression, economic deterioration, and widespread human suffering. Yet, despite the magnitude of this crisis, sustained and inclusive civil resistance has not emerged at a scale commensurate with the suffering of the population. Why? Yet a third jihadist threat is gestating between these two theaters, inside Ethiopia’s Oromia Regional State, largely outside the international radar screen. The movement may not yet have reached the level of organization, operational capacity or visibility necessary to attract the attention of international jihadist networks. However, its ideological undercurrents, recruitment patterns and organizational evolution suggest the beginnings of an embryonic movement — a nascent pulse of jihadist mobilization beating beneath the surface and emitting the early signs of gathering momentum. It warrants noting neither al-Shabaab nor ISIS-Somalia emerged fully formed. Both evolved within particular political, economic and social environments that enabled their emergence and eventual expansion. Their development was shaped not only by extremist ideology but also by institutional weaknesses, insecurity and socioeconomic conditions in the societies where they took root. The central argument of this article is that Oromia may be approaching a more dangerous convergence of political, security and socioeconomic conditions for jihadist expansion than regional and international observers recognize. The underlying ethnic conflict, the region’s enormous population and territorial expanse, and the weakening capacity of the Ethiopian state to exercise effective control make the emerging jihadist insurgency difficult to contain. What is even more alarming is that, as ethnic politics increasingly lost its currency as an instrument of polarization and divide-and-rule, PM Abiy began relying more heavily on religious actors. The contrast between the Somali government’s declared campaign against al-Shabaab and Abiy’s policy of accommodation toward Islamic extremists is particularly troubling. His close association with leaders of radical Islamic movements, coupled with his administration’s failure to prosecute individuals implicated in jihadist violence, has created a no-man’s land for radical Islamists to exploit. The U.S. government’s International Religious Freedom Report has documented allegations of extrajudicial killings of Christians involving Ethiopian government security forces, raising further questions about the state’s role in aiding and abetting religiously motivated violence. Even more troubling is the political and socioeconomic environment in which this threat is developing. Ethiopia’s increasingly fractured political landscape, accumulated politicized grievances, deteriorating security apparatus and expanding mass poverty create conditions potentially conducive to jihadist recruitment and radicalization. There are already scattered indications that extremist networks may be seeking to exploit these conditions, some of which have been documented by international observers. The First Fire: Ethnic Conflict Changing Its Creed The tribalization of conflict has been entrenched in Oromo politics for over half a century. Since Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed took office, law and security have deteriorated sharply across the Oromo tribal homeland. Orthodox Christian communities have faced repeated killings, attacks on churches, destruction of homes and forced displacement. The pattern of rapidly growing violence in East Arsi represents a particularly troubling development. Religion is increasingly overtaking ethnicity as an ideological reference point and organizing principle. The distinction between ethnic and religious conflict matters. Ethnic conflict, however destructive, tends to remain relatively bounded by ethnic identities and political grievances. Religious radicalization transcends those boundaries and attracts external actors, including al-Shabaab and ISIS, who find opportunities to exploit local grievances. The Second Fire: Radical Islam as an Emerging Ideology and Organizing Principle Oromo nationalism once supplied much of the organizing energy of Ethiopian opposition politics. That energy is increasingly struggling to sustain a constituency when communities face economic hardship, displacement and persistent armed instability, with little tangible political dividend to show for it. This is one opening through which Islamic radicalism has entered the political field, drawing on both domestic grievances and transnational ideological networks. There are already identifiable ideological indicators pointing to the nascent formation of an Islamic radical movement. A 2023 study by the U.S. Military Academy’s Combating Terrorism Center, titled The Islamic State Somalia Propaganda Coalition’s Regional Language Pus h, documented a deliberate expansion of pro-ISIS media networks targeting Somali-, Oromo-, Amharic- and Swahili-speaking audiences. The study documents not merely the translation of propaganda but the development of interconnected media networks designed to facilitate ideological indoctrination, recruitment, fundraising, and violent incitement. The Oromo space is more impacted by this campaign, as suggested by the scale and breadth of religion-based violence in the region. This was not simply the occasional translation of extremist material. The researchers identified an emerging propaganda ecosystem comprising dedicated translation outlets, media channels and interactive online networks disseminating ISIS ideological and religious material. The networks operated across platforms including Facebook, Telegram, YouTube and WhatsApp. Of particular significance was Al-Hijrateyn, a pro-ISIS media network producing and distributing Oromo-, Somali- and Swahili-language propaganda. The controversial Indian televangelist and proponent of political Islam, Zakir Naik, is among the prominent transnational preachers whose lectures have circulated among Oromo-speaking audiences. His teachings extend beyond ordinary religious conservatism into a more overtly ideological conception of Islam, raising questions about the potential influence of transnational Islamist narratives on an already politically fractured society. Naik supports the death penalty for apostasy and argues against non-Muslims being permitted to build or repair houses of worship in Muslim-majority states. He also advocates an Islamic political order and rejects Muslim allegiance to secular or minority-led governments. Naik’s teachings supply an ideological vocabulary through which claims of religious superiority can evolve into justifications for violence. This is precisely the ideological progression that extremist mobilizers seek to exploit. It is also precisely the paradigm that figures associated with the Ethiopian radical Islamist movement led by Ahmedin Jabel appear to be drawing on—exploiting it to politicize religious identity and perceived grievances, turning them into instruments of political mobilization and confrontation. Naik’s message is not dependent on conventional religious institutions. His lectures circulate through social media platforms, most importantly in Oromigna. Local preachers can reproduce the format and message, while digital platforms deliver it directly to young audiences. That matters because political radicalization no longer requires a formal organization. A mosque, madrasa, Telegram channel, TikTok account or informal religious network can become a node of mobilization. Naik’s transnational message acts as an accelerator. The Third Fire: Networks Across the Red Sea Oromia’s vulnerability becomes more consequential because it does not exist in isolation. There are already identifiable transnational extremist networks operating in the region. Al-Shabaab has maintained a presence in southeastern Ethiopia since its July 2022 incursion. Sahan Global’s assessment of Jaysh al-Habash estimates that more than 2,500 al-Shabaab fighters took part in the July 2022 incursion, which lasted about 10 days. Although Ethiopian and Somali regional forces repelled much of the assault, several hundred fighters are believed to have remained in southeastern Ethiopia. Sahan estimates that approximately 1,500 subsequently embedded themselves across parts of Bale, Liban and Afdheer. The assessment says the group prioritized recruitment and the development of militant networks over high-profile attacks, identifies the remote Bale Mountains as an area of particular interest, and reports efforts to recruit Salafi converts in remote Borana communities. Al-Shabaab has demonstrated an ability to exploit Ethiopia’s internal conflicts to establish recruitment networks and operational footholds beyond Somalia. Its strategy in southeastern Ethiopia has included recruiting from displaced and economically marginalized communities and cultivating relationships with local religious figures. The Islamic State-Somalia network presents another concern. A 2024 Combating Terrorism Center analysis, drawing on a Somali security source, reported that Ethiopians were among the largest foreign-recruit populations and that the group had recruited ethnic Oromo and Amhara fighters as well as Somali-Ethiopians. The International Crisis Group has independently identified Ethiopia among the countries most frequently cited as origins of foreign recruits. These are attributed intelligence and field assessments, not a verified census of the group’s membership; the evidence supports the presence of Ethiopian recruits, including reported Oromo recruits, rather than a complete regional recruitment profile. ISIS-Linked Networks Operating Inside Ethiopia are not Merely Hypothetical A December 2025 report by the U.N. Security Council’s Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team recorded Ethiopia’s announcement of the 82 arrests and stated that the individuals had been trained by ISIS-Somalia and involved in intelligence, financial and logistical support for the group. The U.N. report corroborates the announcement and places it in the wider regional threat picture. Independent field reporting by Inkstick in November 2025 reveals another dimension. Its investigation, “Along Somalia’s Overlooked Migration Trail, Dangers Lie in Wait,” documented the vulnerability of Ethiopian migrants moving through Puntland, the presence of Ethiopian foreign fighters in ISIS-Somalia’s ranks and the recruitment risks facing stranded migrants in and around Bosaso. The Migration Corridor is Especially Important According to the International Organization for Migration, 234,015 exit movements from Ethiopia were tracked along the Eastern Route in 2024, a 27% increase over 2023. During the same period, tracked transit movements increased by 56% in Djibouti and 23% in Somalia. Across the route, IOM tracked 446,194 movements in 2024; it reported that 89% were driven by economic reasons and 7% by conflict, violence or persecution. Inkstick’s investigation documented how vulnerable Ethiopian migrants stranded in and around Bosaso are exposed to exploitation by traffickers and armed groups. Puntland officials and an International Crisis Group researcher described how ISIS-linked operatives may exploit migrants’ desperation by offering money, food, protection or work in exchange for logistical assistance, with some potentially drawn toward military training. The article also recounts an Arsi migrant’s account of being taken to a military camp and forced to train without pay before fleeing. The implications are serious. Recruitment does not always begin with ideological conviction. For people who are hungry, stranded, financially desperate or fleeing conflict, the initial attraction may be money, food, shelter or protection. Ideological indoctrination can follow material dependence. The transnational dimension extends beyond recruitment. ISIS-Somalia has developed a financial infrastructure that makes it more consequential than its relatively modest territorial footprint might suggest. How the Three Fires Could Meet and Combust The convergence of the above-discussed three fires is what makes the emerging Islamic threat particularly dangerous. They are not necessarily components of a single coordinated movement today. Rather, they are parallel developments that could reinforce one another. There is another political development that deserves attention: the campaign by Ahmedin Jabel and his associates to institutionalize religious identity within Ethiopia’s constitutional and political architecture. Ahmedin argues that citizenship alone cannot adequately address historical religious and cultural marginalization and calls for constitutional recognition of collective religious institutions. His proposal goes beyond protecting religious freedom or ensuring equal representation. It calls for amending the Constitution to introduce religion as an additional political or institutional organizing principle alongside ethnic federalism. Under the current constitutional framework, sovereignty, state ownership and the right to self-determination are vested in the tribal homelands, with ethnic identity forming the basis of the regional-state structure. The foundational principle of Ahmedin Jebel’s proposal is that it seeks to introduce a second axis of political sovereignty into a constitutional order already organized around ethnic self-determination. But how can two competing centers of sovereignty coexist in Oromia? Oromummaa’s “I am first Oromo above my religion” allegiance seeks to transcend religious boundaries, while some of its advocates regard Waaqeffannaa as the indigenous spiritual pillar of Oromo civilization. In Ahmedin’s world, would Oromo Muslims and Christians owe their primary political allegiance to their respective religious constituencies or to the Oromo national community? This would fundamentally transform the Ethiopian constitutional order, moving away from an ethnic-federal model toward a dual identity-based system in which both ethnicity and faith become formal pillars of political organization. Rather than resolving competing identity-based claims, it risks creating yet another constitutional framework for competing claims to political power. There is another dimension to Ahmedin’s campaign that provides a glimpse of Ahmedin’s strategy. His camp advances claims that Muslims constitute the majority of Ethiopia’s population and translates and widely circulates Zakir Naik’s lectures, including his positions restricting the construction and repair of churches in Muslim-majority countries. The recent division of Oromia into six administrative clusters also raises questions about the institutionalization of religious identity. The arrangement has been described as comprising four predominantly Muslim clusters administered by Muslim officials and two predominantly Christian clusters in which Christians control the levers of regional administration. This is the very religious division that Ahmedin’s constitutional proposal seeks to elevate. There is a fundamental difference between protecting religious communities and organizing political authority around religious blocs. The former is a constitutional obligation. The latter risks turning religious identity into another instrument of political competition, territorial bargaining and political power. In Oromia, this debate intersects with the political philosophy of Oromummaa, whose proponents often present Waaqeffannaa, an indigenous Oromo identity, as an overarching national bond transcending religious divisions, and see Islam as an invader. Conclusion: Extinguishing the Fires Before They Become an Inferno Calling the emerging threat Al-Oromia may be premature because the evidence does not yet establish a unified domestic jihadist organization with a clear chain of command, sustained territorial presence and demonstrated operational capacity. But early warning is not limited to identifying a fully formed organization. It requires recognizing the conditions, networks and recruitment pathways that could allow one to emerge. Ignoring those warning signs would amount to a reckless disregard of a potentially serious security threat. The Combating Terrorism Center has documented the multilingual propaganda infrastructure. The United Nations has documented recruitment intermediaries, transportation networks and financial facilitators operating through Puntland. IOM has documented the scale of migration along the Eastern Route and the substantial displacement burden in Oromia. ACLED and the EHRC have documented patterns of civilian targeting and attacks on religious sites in Arsi. Inkstick has reported firsthand accounts of vulnerable Ethiopian migrants and Ethiopian foreign fighters in the Puntland environment. Taken together, these sources establish sufficient warning indicators. The international community should be mindful of the danger associated with the possible emergence of Al-Oromia and look beyond the familiar security theaters of the Red Sea and Somalia. The space between them is not merely a geographic corridor. It is a potential human, ideological, financial and logistical bridge through which extremist networks could penetrate an increasingly fragile Ethiopian state. The three fires have not yet merged. But combustible materials are accumulating, and the political and security conditions for their convergence are becoming increasingly visible. The greatest danger is that, by the time the international community recognizes the threat, the conditions that made it possible may have become too deeply entrenched to reverse. ethiopia.summary: A concerning jihadist movement is emerging in Ethiopia's Oromia Regional State, largely unnoticed by international observers. While attention is focused on threats like al-Shabaab in Somalia, Oromia is experiencing a nascent pulse of jihadist mobilization fueled by political, security, and socioeconomic instability. The Ethiopian government's reliance on religious actors, coupled with a lack of accountability for jihadist violence, has created an environment conducive to radicalization. Ethnic conflicts are increasingly being overshadowed by religious ideologies, with extremist networks exploiting local grievances. The rise of transnational extremist propaganda, particularly from pro-ISIS media targeting Oromo speakers, signals a shift in recruitment strategies. Al-Shabaab and ISIS-Somalia have already established footholds in the region, further complicating the security landscape. The deteriorating political climate and mass poverty in Ethiopia are likely to exacerbate these threats, making it crucial for regional and international stakeholders to recognize and address the emerging jihadist dynamics in Oromia.

ethiopia.content: KDF team detonates three RPG explosives near Kenya-Ethiopia border amid crisis - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME SECURITY KDF team detonates three RPG explosives near Kenya-Ethiopia border amid crisis Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ by CYRUS OMBATI Friday November 13, 2026 IG Kanja in Moyale A team of Kenya Defence Forces (KDF) personnel safely detonated three rocket-propelled grenades (RPGs) discovered near the Kenya-Ethiopia border in the Sessi area of Moyale, Marsabit County. The detonation was the second exercise in two weeks, officials said amid a growing crisis. The explosives, which had no visible registration markings, were destroyed on Monday, November 9, following reports that two RPGs had landed near a slaughter site close to the border. The two explosives, fitted with stabilising fins at the rear, were reportedly fired from Ethiopia at around 2 am Monday before landing a few metres inside Kenyan territory, officials said. KDF officers based in Moyale carried out the controlled demolition, with no injuries or property damage reported. advertisements On their way back from the demolition site, the soldiers discovered a third RPG along the roadside near Sessi Mixed Secondary School. The third explosive, which did not have stabilising fins, was also safely detonated. Authorities said they had increased security personnel in the area to address the growing crisis. The explosives are being launched by rival groups targeting those seeking refuge in Kenyan side. The government has confirmed that approximately 40,000 Ethiopians have crossed into Kenya and are currently being hosted in Moyale following escalating tensions in parts of Ethiopia. Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi said tensions in Ethiopia had forced thousands of people to flee into Kenya. "The issue is that from the Ethiopian side, they have been having a little bit of tension over there. So, the problem has caused about 40,000 people to evacuate to Kenya," he said. Mudavadi said he had communicated with his Ethiopian counterpart and asked him to intervene and help stabilise the situation so that the displaced families can return home. "I told him to try and calm the situation in their country so that the refugees return to their homes," he said. He added that the Ethiopian government had assured Kenya that it was working to restore normalcy. "They have assured us that they will do their best to return the issues to normalcy and then the people can go back," Mudavadi said. The displacement follows clashes that erupted in October 2026, amid longstanding disagreements between the Oromia and Somali regional administrations over territorial boundaries and administrative control. The fighting has displaced thousands of people, with many families seeking shelter in schools, churches and temporary camps, while others have been accommodated by relatives and members of the local community. Inspector General of Police Douglas Kanja ordered the deployment of additional police officers to Moyale, Marsabit County, amid growing security concerns linked to developments in neighbouring Ethiopia. Kanja announced the reinforcement on November 5, during a security assessment visit to the border town, where he chaired a strategic meeting with regional security commanders to review the prevailing security situation. He directed officers deployed in the area to remain on high alert and strengthen surveillance to protect residents and their property. The Inspector General assured residents that the National Police Service (NPS) was committed to maintaining peace and stability in the region through enhanced security operations. “We are here to ensure all the visitors and locals are safe. We will ensure more personnel arrive for protection,” he said. He also urged members of the public to cooperate with security agencies by providing timely and relevant information that could help prevent security threats. Kanja toured a camp hosting families displaced by insecurity, where he assured them of enhanced protection and coordinated humanitarian assistance in partnership with relief agencies. The security assessment comes amid concerns over instability in neighbouring Ethiopia and its potential implications for security along Kenya's northern border. Kanja was accompanied by Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI) Director Mohammed Amin, General Service Unit (GSU) Commandant Johanna Tonui and Kenya Police Service Director of Operations Philip Opiyo. Others present included Eastern Regional Commissioner Jacob Muganda, Eastern Regional Police Commander Stephen Chebet, Eastern Regional Administration Police Commander Michael Owino and Regional Criminal Investigations Officer Michael Sang, alongside other senior security officials. The visit came a day after a 20-year-old woman was seriously injured after being struck by two suspected stray bullets believed to have originated from neighbouring Ethiopia in Moyale, Marsabit County. The incident occurred on November 4, 2026, at approximately 12:15pm while the victim was at her home in Biashara area. Police said she was hit by two bullets in the back, leaving her unconscious. She was rushed to Taqwa Nursing Home Hospital, where medical personnel removed the two bullets. The victim was admitted in serious condition as police documented the incident. The circumstances under which the bullets crossed into Kenyan territory remain unclear. This is the latest such incident in the area amid growing crisis due to ongoing fighting in Ethiopia pitting two communities. A 65-year-old woman was killed in the area, after she was reportedly struck by a suspected stray bullet believed to have originated from ongoing clashes in neighbouring Ethiopia. The deceased was identified as Amina Guchi, who was reportedly at the Moyale County offices, located next to Moyale Law Courts, when the incident occurred on November 2, 2026. Guchi was speaking to a security official on duty when an object believed to be a stray bullet struck her on the head from behind. She collapsed and lost consciousness before being rushed to Moyale Sub-County Referral Hospital, where she was pronounced dead on arrival. Police officers subsequently visited the hospital, where a post-mortem examination was conducted before the body was released to the family for burial arrangements. The neighbouring Moyale is experiencing conflict which has displaced more than 50,000 people. Security officers in the area had earlier on safely detonated three rocket-propelled grenades (RPGs) that reportedly landed in the area after being discharged from neighbouring Ethiopia. The explosives were discovered on Sunday, November 1, 2026, following a report about unexploded explosive materials that had landed near Sessi Primary School. This affected learning and examinations at the centre. Two Kenya Certificate of Secondary Education (KCSE) examination centres in Moyale Sub-County, Marsabit County, were relocated following the insecurity linked to clan clashes along the Kenya-Ethiopia border. According to police, the explosives were found at two locations- one at Sessi Primary School and two others at the Meteorological Department offices. Police and a team of bomb disposal experts from the Kenya Defence Forces (KDF) based at Odha rushed to the scene. The security team established that the materials were three RPGs, which were subsequently secured, removed and safely detonated by the bomb experts. At least three people had been injured after bullets hit structures in the area two weeks ago. The United Nations refugee agency has warned of growing humanitarian needs in northern Kenya after an estimated 50,000 people fled clashes in Ethiopia and crossed the border into Moyale in search of safety. The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) said significant cross-border movements had been reported since October 22, with the number of arrivals remaining fluid as registration and verification efforts continued. Local authorities estimate that up to 50,000 people have entered Kenya, with reports indicating that additional crossings could further increase the number of people requiring assistance. Many of those fleeing the violence are women and children, raising concerns over their protection and access to essential services. The conflict started three weeks ago following the alleged raising of the flag of the Somali Regional State in Ethiopia, which triggered clashes between forces and groups from the Oromia and Somali regional states. According to UNHCR, some arrivals are staying with relatives and host communities, while others have sought temporary shelter in schools and churches. This incident is part of a broader crisis, with approximately 40,000 Ethiopians fleeing to Kenya due to ongoing conflicts between the Oromia and Somali regional administrations. EST to November 13 at 9:00 A.M. EST. To receive the Africa File, Ethiopia War Security Review, or Congo War Security Review via email, please subscribe here . Follow CTP on X , LinkedIn , and BlueSky for daily updates. Read CTP’s latest analysis on the war in Ethiopia in the weekly Africa File here . Key Takeaways: Northern Axis. Local sources claimed that Amhara Fano National Movement fighters fought alongside Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) forces against Ethiopian federal forces near the Ethiopia-Eritrea border, although the Critical Threats Project (CTP) could not confirm the unverified claims. Western Axis. The Ethiopian military reportedly sustained fighting with TPLF and Eritrean forces around Badme, an Eritrean border town. Central Axis. Ethiopian federal and TPLF forces reportedly clashed in the mountainous Tigray interior south of Axum. Major Domestic Political Developments. The interim Tigray regional government has continued setting up its administration amid internal tensions. Ethiopian security forces are reportedly conducting forced conscription in the Oromia region and Addis Ababa, the Ethiopian capital. Regional and International Activity. Various international actors affirmed their support for de-escalation between Ethiopia and Eritrea, although officials from the two countries have continued to accuse each other of escalation. Figure 1. ENDF and TPLF Battle Across Tigray Note: ENDF stands for Ethiopian National Defense Force. TPLF stands for Tigray People’s Liberation Front. Source: Michael DeAngelo; Liam Karr; Alexander Brown. Eastern Axis: Afar Region Nothing significant to report. Northern Axis: Rama-Zalambessa-Dallol Local sources claimed that Amhara Fano National Movement (AFNM) fighters fought alongside the Tigray Defense Force (TDF), the TPLF’s military wing, against Ethiopian federal forces near the Ethiopia-Eritrea border, although CTP could not confirm the unverified claims. Federal and TDF forces reportedly clashed around Rama, which is approximately 20 miles north of Adwa and just south of the Ethiopia-Eritrea border, on November 7. [1] Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED) reported that federal forces retook Rama, while the TDF claimed to have overcome federal forces and inflicted mass casualties upon them. [2] Fighting between the two sides reportedly broke out again around Rama between November 9 and 11. [3] The Ethiopian news outlet Wazema Radio cited residents who claimed that the AFNM and Afar Revolutionary Democratic Unity Front—both of whom are members of the Alliance for Survival rebel coalition with the TPLF—fought alongside the TDF. [4] Conflict tracker Sajid Nadeem and another conflict tracker on X also reported that the AFNM participated in the fighting, although CTP could not confirm the unverified claims. [5] Western Axis: Humera-Addi Remets-Shire The Ethiopian military (Ethiopian National Defense Force, ENDF) reportedly sustained fighting with TDF and Eritrean forces around Badme, an Eritrean border town. The ENDF reportedly began fighting with TDF and Eritrean forces around the town on November 9 following several days of mutual buildups, although CTP could not verify whether fighting occurred on the Ethiopian or Eritrean side of the border. [6] Wazema Radio and a conflict tracker on X reported that the ENDF and TDF continued clashing on November 10 near Gomahalo, which is an Ethiopian village approximately 20 miles south of Badme. [7] The ENDF and Eritrean military (Eritrean Defense Forces, EDF) reportedly traded artillery fire around Badme from November 11 to 13. [8] The EDNF also reportedly conducted drone strikes on EDF positions. [9] The Ethiopian Conflict Map and Sajid Nadeem claimed that the ENDF captured Badme on November 12, although ACLED reported on November 13 that neither the ENDF nor the EDF controlled the town but that “Eritrean intelligence personnel” had been present. [10] The Ethiopian news outlet Addis Standard cited a resident of Badme who said that ENDF forces have been present in Badme since November 12, however. [11] Central Axis: Abiy Addi-Adwa-Axum Ethiopian federal forces and the TDF reportedly clashed in the mountainous Tigray interior south of Axum. The TDF has contested Ethiopian federal efforts to control areas around Tigray’s city belt since mid-October 2026. [12] The Ethiopian Conflict Map and Sajid Nadeem reported that the two sides clashed near Semema, which is approximately 20 miles south of Axum, on November 11. [13] Southern Axis: Mekele-Alamata-Sekota-Woldia Nothing significant to report. Northern Amhara Sector: From B21 Northward Nothing significant to report. Other Rebel Kinetic Activity Nothing significant to report. Major Domestic Political Developments The interim Tigray regional government has continued setting up its administration amid internal tensions. The interim administration has reportedly faced discord over appointments and governance, including payment of civil servants’ salaries. [14] A conflict tracker on X reported on November 11 that 11 senior members of Ethiopian Prime Ministerial Adviser Getachew Reda’s Simret party, which heavily influences the interim administration, resigned due to the discord. [15] Two conflict trackers separately reported on November 10 that the interim administration appointed Daniel Negash as “coordinator” for the Western Zone, which is disputed by Amhara and Tigrayan communities. [16] Ethiopian security forces are reportedly conducting forced conscription in the Oromia region and Addis Ababa. The Ethiopian Human Rights Commission and Addis Standard previously reported on forced conscription in Oromia in at least December 2024 and August 2026, respectively. [17] Addis Standard and the Canadian news outlet The Globe and Mail cited residents of Oromia and Addis Ababa on November 12 who reported that Ethiopian security forces had forcibly conscripted some of their family members and other civilians. [18] The Globe and Mail cited two residents of Addis Ababa who separately reported that the ENDF had sent their sons to the front lines in Tigray. [19] Addis Standard cited residents of Jimma, one of the largest cities in Oromia, who described forced conscription as a factor that sparked protests against regional and federal authorities on November 9 and 10. [20] Regional and International Activity Various international actors affirmed their support for de-escalation between Ethiopia and Eritrea, although officials from the two countries have continued to accuse each other of escalation. Five Democratic members of the US Senate Foreign Relations Committee sent a letter to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on November 10 that urged Rubio to increase US efforts to mediate between Ethiopia, Ethiopian rebel groups, and Eritrea. [21] The Democratic senators requested that the US State Department avoid offering Eritrea’s port of Assab to Ethiopia in any mediation and discourage Egypt, Eritrea, and Sudan from supporting Ethiopian rebel groups. [22] The Group of Seven (G7) foreign ministers separately released a statement on November 11 after meeting in Paris that expressed “great concern” over tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea and called for “maximum restraint” and “diplomatic solutions.” [23] Special Envoy of the United Nations (UN) Secretary-General for the Horn of Africa Guang Cong met with Getachew on November 11 to discuss the security situation in the Horn of Africa. Cong has previously pledged that the UN will work toward peace and stability in the region. [24] Ethiopian and Eritrean officials have continued to accuse each other of escalation, which has been a pattern since the renewed war in northern Ethiopia began in late September 2026. Getachew posted on X that he discussed the “destructive role the Regime in Asmara is playing in the region” during his meeting with Cong. [25] Getachew also directly accused Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki and Sudanese Transitional Sovereignty Council President Abdel Fattah al Burhan of equipping, arming, and coordinating with Ethiopian rebel groups, including by helping them conduct drone attacks in Ethiopia. [26] Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel posted on X on November 11 that Ethiopia has a “regional” war agenda. ethiopia.content: World Insights: Sudan-Ethiopia tensions escalate amid mutual accusations, raising regional concerns-Xinhua World Insights: Sudan-Ethiopia tensions escalate amid mutual accusations, raising regional concerns Source: Xinhua Editor: huaxia 2026-11-14 05:20:15 This photo taken on Jan. 11, 2025 shows people celebrating the Sudanese army's retaking of Wad Madani, the capital city of Gezira State in central Sudan, in Omdurman, north of the capital Khartoum, Sudan. (Photo by Mohamed Khidir/Xinhua) KHARTOUM, Nov. 13 (Xinhua) -- Relations between Sudan and Ethiopia have entered a new phase of tension, as mutual accusations of interference in internal affairs and support for armed groups have spilled over into diplomatic retaliation and appeals to international and regional bodies. The growing rift has raised concerns over its potential implications for stability in the Horn of Africa. The Sudanese government has accused Ethiopia of allowing its territory to be used as a launching ground for drones targeting Sudan and providing logistical support to the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which have been fighting the Sudanese Armed Forces since April 2023. Khartoum has filed complaints with the UN Security Council and the African Union Peace and Security Council, accusing Addis Ababa of facilitating attacks launched from Ethiopian territory. Ethiopia subsequently closed the Sudanese consulate in Asosa and gave six Sudanese diplomats 48 hours to leave the country. Sudan responded by closing the Ethiopian consulate in Gedaref and expelling its diplomats. Addis Ababa, meanwhile, accused Sudan of providing safe havens and logistical support to fighters from the Tigray People's Liberation Front, which has been engaged in a prolonged confrontation with the Ethiopian government. MUTUAL ACCUSATIONS DEEPEN SECURITY CONCERNS Khalid Dirar, a professor of political science at al-Rasid Center for Strategic Studies in Khartoum, said the diplomatic escalation reflected growing tensions and could lead to further restrictions on official relations. Beyond the diplomatic dispute, the mutual accusations reflect deeper security concerns and competing regional interests, said the observers. Ethiopian political analyst Biniam Niguse noted that Addis Ababa viewed the Sudanese army's repeated accusations and Khartoum's involvement in a regional axis as attempts to encircle Ethiopia and exert pressure on it. Whatever the motives behind them, the recent exchange of accusations reflects growing mistrust between the two countries, with both increasingly concerned about threats to their respective security and political interests. Sudanese political analyst Abdul-Raziq Ziyada warned that the conflicts in Sudan and Ethiopia could become increasingly intertwined, with repercussions extending to neighboring countries. Continued tensions could undermine border security, disrupt population movements and trade, and create opportunities for armed groups to conduct cross-border activities, Niguse cautioned. This photo taken on March 6, 2026 shows an equestrian statue in Mekelle, Tigray region, Ethiopia. (Xinhua/Liu Fangqiang) LONGSTANDING DISPUTES COMPLICATE BILATERAL TIES The current crisis is also rooted in longstanding disagreements over the Fashaga border area, Nile waters and the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam. Ziyada identified the dam and border disputes, particularly over Fashaga, as major sources of tension. The area is strategically important for agriculture and is home to communities with overlapping economic and social interests on both sides of the border. Ethiopian political expert Getachew Abra said Sudan's position on the Renaissance Dam was a source of concern for Addis Ababa. He noted that the dispute had expanded beyond water management to encompass broader political and security considerations. Abra also linked the current tensions to the repercussions of the conflict in the Tigray region, particularly after Sudan strengthened its presence in border areas. He noted that RSF accusations that Tigrayan fighters were participating alongside the Sudanese army had added another dimension to the dispute. He added that Ethiopia's internal conflicts and security challenges had further complicated its relations with neighboring countries. The overlapping conflicts in the two countries, particularly in border areas where armed groups operate, risk turning the shared frontier into a source of insecurity. This photo taken on April 16, 2025 shows the damage to Khartoum Hospital as a result of military clashes between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), in Khartoum, Sudan. (Photo by Mohamed Hamid/Xinhua) MILITARY CONFRONTATION RISKS WIDER CONFLICT Analysts have cautioned that the diplomatic dispute could potentially develop into a direct military confrontation, with implications extending beyond the two countries. In an analysis entitled "Sudan and Ethiopia: A New Front of Confrontation in a Dangerous Situation," the International Center for Strategic Studies warned that any Sudanese military response targeting sites inside Ethiopia, including airports or drone launch facilities, could widen the conflict and turn it into a regional confrontation. Ziyada similarly cautioned that attacks on military sites or facilities inside either country could trigger reciprocal military measures that would be difficult to contain, particularly amid the ongoing conflict in Sudan and overlapping regional interests and alliances. Such escalation could further destabilize the Horn of Africa, where the conflicts in Sudan and Ethiopia intersect with Nile water disputes and competition among regional powers. Addressing border security and non-interference in internal affairs, while maintaining political and diplomatic communication, were essential to containing the crisis and safeguarding stability across the Horn of Africa, Ziyada said. ■ Comments Comments (0) Send You may like Miao ethnic group celebrates Miao New Year in SW China's Guizhou Media center for 2026 APEC Economic Leaders' Week opens in Shenzhen, China's Guangdong Top honors unveiled at China's Golden Rooster Awards Highlights of cultural events at 9th CIIE Shenzhen Int'l Garden and Flower Expo Park reopens after renovations 9th China International Import Expo concludes in Shanghai More from GLOBALink Experts highlight APEC's role in boosting regional cooperation, trade stability China's green development wins praise at COP31 An American man's decades-long bond with a Chinese county Follow us on More from GLOBALink Experts highlight APEC's role in boosting regional cooperation, trade stability China's green development wins praise at COP31 An American man's decades-long bond with a Chinese county Follow us on World Insights: Sudan-Ethiopia tensions escalate amid mutual accusations, raising regional concerns
