The return of Joseph Kabila: What it does – and doesn’t – mean for Congo’s war Home Uncategorized Abiy Ahmed’s Red Sea Obsession and the Politics of Manufactured Grievances Uncategorized Abiy Ahmed’s Red Sea Obsession and the Politics of Manufactured Grievances Yohannes Woldemariam 2 days ago 2 days ago 14 mins H.E. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed at the African Union/ CREDIT: Office of the Prime Minister - Ethiopia Abiy Ahmed is preparing Ethiopians to accept a dangerous idea: that their country’s future depends on acquiring territory on the Red Sea, even if that means another war with Eritrea. What began as occasional statements about Ethiopia’s maritime ambitions has become a persistent political campaign. Former national leaders, academics, lawyers, state media and numerous online commentators are repeating the same message. Ethiopia has supposedly suffered an injustice that must be corrected. But what exactly is this injustice, and who is responsible for it? The timing deserves attention. Ethiopia is facing serious internal conflicts, economic hardship and growing questions about Abiy’s authority. Yet instead of addressing these problems, the government has elevated the Red Sea into a question of national survival. At the Tana Forum in October 2026 , Abiy described the maritime question as existential. His language has become increasingly troubling, particularly when he suggests that Ethiopia will become a Red Sea power by one means or another. The people who would pay the price of another war are not those making these declarations. They are ordinary Eritreans and Ethiopians, many of whom have already lost family members in successive conflicts. What makes this campaign especially disturbing is the attempt to manufacture a grievance where none exists. Ethiopia did not lose Assab in 1993. Eritrea recovered its independence after thirty years of struggle. Yet Ethiopian politicians and intellectuals increasingly present Eritrea’s independence as though Ethiopia had been robbed of territory that rightfully belonged to it. The history of a people who fought to free themselves from Ethiopian rule is being rewritten as an Ethiopian national tragedy. The sacrifices of Eritreans, who lost parents, children, brothers and sisters, almost disappear from this narrative. I believe Ethiopia is experiencing the decay of an imperial political order whose contradictions have never been resolved. Abiy did not invent the imperial nostalgia that makes such claims possible. But he is exploiting it at a particularly dangerous moment, when his own political survival is increasingly uncertain. His Red Sea obsession is not a solution to Ethiopia’s problems. It is an attempt to redirect attention from them. An empire in decline cannot save itself by acquiring another piece of territory. Consider the arguments now being advanced about Assab. Assegid “AZ” Habtewold, in his essay Ethiopia Has a Real Grievance Over Assab. A War Would Not Fix It , opposes war but accepts the premise that Ethiopia has a legitimate grievance. Yacob Hailemariam goes further. In a December 2025 interview with The Reporter , he argued that Assab was never part of Eritrea and blamed Ethiopian leaders for failing to retain it. Although their conclusions differ, both begin with Ethiopia’s supposed loss rather than Eritrea’s recovery of independence. There is a remarkable historical irony. Assab was where the territorial formation of modern Eritrea began. In 1869, the Italian Rubattino Shipping Company began acquiring holdings around the Bay of Assab from local Afar authorities. The Italian government took over those holdings in 1882, occupied Massawa in 1885 and formally established Eritrea as a colony in 1890. This history is recorded in the Eritrea–Ethiopia Boundary Commission’s April 2002 decision . The Afar people, of course, had their own institutions and political relationships long before Italian colonialism. Their communities extend across today’s international boundary. But this older history does not establish Ethiopian sovereignty over Assab. The legal arguments deserve particular attention because some of those advancing them are trained lawyers. The Eritrea–Ethiopia Boundary Commission included distinguished international jurists, among them Stephen Schwebel, a former president of the International Court of Justice, and Sir Elihu Lauterpacht, who chaired the commission. Under Article 4 of the Algiers Agreement of December 2000 , Ethiopia and Eritrea agreed that their common boundary would be determined according to the colonial treaties of 1900, 1902 and 1908 and applicable international law. Both accepted that the commission’s decisions would be final and binding. The commission did not grant Eritrea independence, nor was it asked to decide whether Ethiopia should receive Assab. Eritrea was already internationally recognized following the 1993 referendum, in which more than 99 percent of participating voters supported independence. The commission was established to determine the boundary between two sovereign countries after their devastating war of 1998 to 2000. There is a wider African principle involved here. In 1964, the Organization of African Unity adopted the Cairo Resolution affirming respect for boundaries inherited at independence. African leaders were not declaring that colonial borders were fair or that colonial conquest deserved approval. They understood that reopening territorial disputes according to competing claims of historical ownership could condemn the continent to endless wars. The distinguished Somali jurist Abdulqawi Ahmed Yusuf, who later served as president of the International Court of Justice, made an important distinction in his separate opinion in the Burkina Faso–Niger frontier case . He distinguished the African commitment to respecting inherited boundaries from the classical doctrine of uti possidetis juris . The African position was not simply about legitimizing colonial territorial arrangements. It was also a deliberate choice to preserve territorial stability among newly independent states. This distinction is particularly relevant to Ethiopia. The modern Ethiopian state was constructed partly through conquest and territorial incorporation. Under Menelik II, territories inhabited by Oromo, Sidama, Wolayta, Somali and other peoples were brought into the expanding empire. What Ethiopian nationalist history celebrates as unification was experienced by many of those communities as conquest, dispossession and loss of political autonomy. The history of conquest and resistance among the Arsi Oromo illustrates this process. If historical possession becomes the basis for revising internationally recognized boundaries, Ethiopia would expose its own territorial integrity to similar arguments. A principle cannot be valid when it enlarges a country and suddenly become irrelevant when it might make that country smaller. Eritrea followed a different historical and legal path. It was federated with Ethiopia in 1952 under a United Nations arrangement. Haile Selassie progressively dismantled that federation and annexed Eritrea in 1962. Eritreans resisted until Ethiopian rule ended in 1991. The fact that successive Ethiopian governments administered Eritrea, stationed troops there and encouraged settlement cannot create a permanent right to rule Eritreans against their will. How can someone take possession of another person’s property and then claim to be the victim when the rightful owner retrieves it? Sovereignty is not private property, but the analogy exposes the contradiction. The events following independence also undermine the manufactured grievance. The Eritrean People’s Liberation Front emerged from thirty years of war in an exceptionally strong military position. It defeated Ethiopian forces in Eritrea and helped the TPLF and other Ethiopian opposition movements overthrow the Derg. Rather than seeking Ethiopia’s fragmentation, the EPLF cooperated with the new authorities in Addis Ababa. That cooperation extended to Assab. A 1995 International Monetary Fund report confirms that Assab operated as a free port for Ethiopia following Eritrean independence. Ethiopia maintained its own customs office, and goods moving to and from the country were exempt from Eritrean customs duties and related charges. Much of Ethiopia’s international trade continued through Assab until war broke out in 1998. Ethiopia did not lose the ability to use Assab in 1993. It ceased exercising sovereignty over Eritrean territory while retaining substantial commercial privileges. The two countries demonstrated that Eritrean sovereignty and Ethiopian economic interests could coexist. Meles Zenawi did not give Assab away. Eritrea was not his to give. The manufactured grievance has nevertheless entered academic scholarship. In a 2025 article in Mizan Law Review , Biruk Paulos and Temesgen Thomas Halabo examine Ethiopia’s historical administration of Assab and the rights of landlocked states. These are legitimate subjects for legal discussion, but historical administration cannot simply be transformed into permanent territorial ownership. Other Ethiopian legal scholars disagree with territorial incorporation. Professor Dereje Zeleke Mekonnen rejected such a proposal in a 2019 interview . Mahemud Eshtu Tekuya similarly argued in the Fordham International Law Journal that Ethiopia has no legitimate sovereign claim over Assab, while recognizing its rights as a landlocked country. What concerns me is that the campaign is no longer confined to academic discussions. In October 2026, former Prime Minister Hailemariam Desalegn described Ethiopia’s separation from the Red Sea as a historical scar , although he advocated negotiations. Former President Mulatu Teshome also made statements linking Ethiopia’s maritime claims to its confrontation with Eritrea. I do not believe these interventions should be treated as isolated coincidences. Hailemariam has generally maintained a low public profile and rarely intervenes in major political controversies. Why has he chosen this particular moment to speak about Ethiopia’s supposed grievance over the Red Sea? His intervention, together with that of Mulatu, raises questions about whether former national leaders are participating in a broader effort to give Abiy’s territorial ambitions the appearance of national consensus. The same manufactured grievance is repeated by current and former leaders, amplified by state media and circulated through numerous YouTube channels. There are also allegations that online commentators have been paid to promote this narrative, although the scale and financing of such activity require independent verification. Whether all these voices are formally coordinated remains to be established. But repetition has its own political effect. A manufactured grievance begins to acquire the appearance of truth, not because new historical or legal evidence has emerged, but because influential figures repeat it until it becomes familiar. There is another historical irony. Mulatu comes from Wollega in Oromia, while Hailemariam comes from Wolayta. Both regions were incorporated into the Ethiopian Empire during Menelik’s expansion. Their origins do not determine their political positions, but the contrast deserves examination. Why is the incorporation of their regions celebrated as national unification, while Eritrea’s recovery of independence is presented as a national wound? Beating the drums of war against Eritrea also appears to have become a means of political rehabilitation. Figures who once challenged Ethiopian centralism, including some who opposed Abiy himself, are discovering common ground in territorial nationalism. The Red Sea question offers an opportunity to appear patriotic without confronting the imperial assumptions behind their demands. Jawar Mohammed is a revealing example. Once a prominent advocate of Oromo nationalism and a fierce critic of Abiy, he has promoted a campaign called “Now or Never.” In an interview on 28 October 2026 with AFP , he argued that Ethiopia should act while it enjoys a military and technological advantage, before Eritrea strengthens its defenses. This is not a proposal for peaceful commercial cooperation. It is an argument for exploiting a perceived military opportunity against a sovereign neighboring country. Jawar built much of his political reputation by challenging Ethiopian centralism. Political positions can change, but such a reversal deserves an explanation. Why should the history of Ethiopian domination, once central to his arguments, suddenly become irrelevant when the proposed victims of territorial expansion are Eritreans? Not everything proclaimed as a national interest deserves recognition as a legitimate one. A demand for the invasion of a sovereign neighbor cannot be dignified simply because it is wrapped in patriotism. The United Nations Charter prohibits the threat or use of force against another state’s territorial integrity or political independence, except under narrowly defined legal exceptions. Those promoting military action should explain why another generation of poor Eritrean and Ethiopian families must sacrifice their children for an ambition that cannot resolve Ethiopia’s internal problems. Ethiopia’s modern political history is, in important respects, a succession of attempts to preserve an inherited state without resolving the political aspirations of its peoples. Haile Selassie’s imperial order collapsed in 1974. The Derg attempted to preserve centralized rule through military force and revolutionary ideology but fell in 1991. The EPRDF promised a different arrangement through ethnic federalism, yet its own system of political domination eventually faced a crisis. Abiy came to power amid that breakdown, promising reform and reconciliation. The conflicts in Tigray, Amhara and Oromia have different histories and objectives. Yet they reveal how deeply contested the character of the Ethiopian state remains. Questions about political autonomy, the distribution of power and the legitimacy of centralized authority have not disappeared simply because governments have changed. I believe Abiy increasingly sees the Red Sea question as important to his political survival. Faced with serious challenges at home, he has revived a manufactured grievance and presented it as a national cause that should unite Ethiopians behind his government. It is easier to rally people against an external enemy than to answer difficult questions about political legitimacy and the future of the state. At the Tana Forum on October 24, 2026 , Abiy described the maritime question as an existential matter connected to Ethiopia’s security and future generations. He spoke of dialogue and mutual benefit while proclaiming that Ethiopia would become a Red Sea power through “Bale or Bolle,” an expression suggesting by hook or crook. An economic question is being elevated into a matter of national survival, creating the impression that Ethiopia cannot have a future without acquiring control over territory beyond its internationally recognized borders. In an October 30 interview on the International Crisis Group’s The Horn , Reuters journalist Giulia Paravicini discussed her visit to Asmara and fears among Eritrean officials that Ethiopia might attack Assab. These fears cannot be separated from the history of Ethiopian annexation and the long struggle Eritreans fought to recover their independence. Four days after the Tana Forum, Abiy announced the acquisition of twelve Russian Su-35 fighter jets and plans for four S-400 air defense batteries. Although he referred to twelve aircraft, the Russian arms exporter told Reuters that the first batch consisted of two. The financial terms have not been disclosed. I find the celebration of expensive military equipment particularly disturbing when millions of Ethiopians struggle to meet their basic needs. It reminds me of someone suffering from a life-threatening illness who decides to spen
ethiopia.summary: Abiy Ahmed's recent focus on Ethiopia's territorial ambitions in the Red Sea has raised concerns about the potential for renewed conflict with Eritrea. This political campaign, which frames Ethiopia's maritime aspirations as a matter of national survival, has gained traction among various political and intellectual circles. However, critics argue that this narrative is an attempt to manufacture grievances where none exist, particularly regarding the historical context of Eritrea's independence in 1993. The Ethiopian government is accused of diverting attention from pressing internal issues, such as economic hardship and political instability, by promoting a narrative of loss and injustice related to Assab. This perspective overlooks the sacrifices made by Eritreans during their struggle for independence and risks perpetuating a cycle of conflict. The article emphasizes the importance of respecting established international boundaries to maintain stability in the region and warns against the dangers of reviving historical territorial claims.

ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Should Join Regional Mechanisms to Safeguard Red Sea Security: French, Danish Defense Attachés - ENA English - ENA Skip to Content Ethiopia Should Join Regional Mechanisms to Safeguard Red Sea Security: French, Danish Defense Attachés - ENA English Live: አማርኛ ትግርኛ Afaan Oromoo Af‑Soomaali Qafar Afa English Français عربي Politics Social Economy Sport Technology Environment Feature Videos About Us Ethiopia Should Join Regional Mechanisms to Safeguard Red Sea Security: French, Danish Defense Attachés 🔇Unmute Addis Ababa, November 13, 2026 (ENA)— French and Danish Defense Attachés underscored Ethiopia’s legitimate interest in Red Sea access and its potential role in safeguarding maritime security and combating terrorism in the strategically important Horn of Africa. Speaking to ENA, the defense attachés also said as a regional power, Ethiopia should get involved in mechanisms that can provide global security in the Horn of Africa. French Defense Attaché Colonel Damien Cypryk said Ethiopia’s aspiration for access to the Red Sea is legitimate, given its importance to the country's development and stability. “Access to the Red Sea for Ethiopia is a perfectly legitimate act because it is a question of development and stability,” he stated. Currently, Ethiopia is actively pursuing permanent access to the Red Sea, citing its geographical, historical and economic circumstances. The country’s geographical proximity to the Red Sea, together with its historical links to the region’s ports, has remained central to its push for securing a sovereign sea outlet. Cypryk underscored the strategic importance of the Red Sea, the Bab al-Mandab Strait, and the Horn of Africa, describing them as a vital corridor whose security has far-reaching implications beyond the region. He noted that developments in this strategically significant area could have repercussions across the African continent and the wider international community. The defense attaché stressed that Ethiopia, as a regional power, has a legitimate role to play in regional security and should actively participate in mechanisms designed to safeguard peace and stability. “I am convinced that Ethiopia, as a regional power, is absolutely legitimate to contribute to regional security, and it should get involved in mechanisms that can provide security in the region,” he said. The French Defense Attaché further explained that France supports dialogue and negotiations as the appropriate means of addressing Ethiopia’s quest for sea access, noting that Paris, like many other countries, has strategic interests in the region and therefore promotes peace and stability. On his part, Danish Defense Attaché to Ethiopia Commander Anders Lakjer highlighted Ethiopia’s potential contribution to combating terrorism and addressing growing threats to maritime security in the region. “Ethiopia can play a very important role in terms of fighting terrorism and also all the threats against maritime security in the area,” he told ENA. Lakjer called on countries capable of contributing to regional security to work together to strengthen maritime protection and counterterrorism efforts. © Ethiopian News Agency 2023 Hidden
ethiopia.summary: French and Danish Defense Attachés have emphasized Ethiopia's legitimate interest in accessing the Red Sea and its potential role in enhancing maritime security in the Horn of Africa. They highlighted that Ethiopia's pursuit of permanent access to the Red Sea is crucial for its development and stability, given its geographical and historical ties to the region. French Defense Attaché Colonel Damien Cypryk noted the strategic significance of the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab Strait, asserting that Ethiopia should actively engage in regional security mechanisms. He advocated for dialogue and negotiations to address Ethiopia's sea access aspirations. Danish Defense Attaché Commander Anders Lakjer underscored Ethiopia's capacity to combat terrorism and maritime threats, urging collaboration among nations to bolster regional security. Both attachés stressed the importance of Ethiopia's involvement in safeguarding peace and stability in this vital corridor, which has implications beyond the region.

ethiopia.title: Ethiopia's Tigray conflict: Has Abiy Ahmed defeated the TPLF? - BBC
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia's Tigray conflict: Has Abiy Ahmed defeated the TPLF? Skip to content Watch Live British Broadcasting Corporation Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Neither war nor peace in Tigray - is Ethiopia's latest conflict really over? 2 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Michael Teferi , BBC Africa and Yemane Nagish , BBC Tigrinya AFP via Getty Images Pro-government forces marched into Tigray's capital less than two weeks after the war began Running a hair salon in Mekelle, capital of Ethiopia's troubled northern Tigray region, is not easy at the moment. "People can't prioritise beauty over daily basic needs. For many residents, thinking about self-care is a luxury, at a time when they can't feed their kids," Firut Me'ar, who runs a salon in the city, tells the BBC. After a brief war, the city is under the control of the national army but life is far from normal, says Firut, a single mother of a 10-year-old daughter. "Things are better than during the war, but people still have no money, no morale. Business is almost non-existent," she says, her voice shaking with emotion. Above all, she says people are worried about what the future holds. "There is uncertainty about what comes next." Fighting broke out in late September between the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that had run Tigray for decades, and the national army - a resumption of the two-year civil war that officially ended in 2022. But within less than two weeks, federal forces marched triumphantly into Mekelle. The TPLF made what it called a "strategic withdrawal" from the city and Tigray's other main towns so the army encountered little resistance. Hundreds of people are reported to have died in the conflict, including dozens killed by drone strikes and bombing raids by the air force. Ethiopian government officials and supporters argue that the war is effectively over and that the only remaining task is to clear Tigray of TPLF elements. Getachew Reda, a senior TPLF official who switched sides and is now an adviser to the prime minister, declared that the war in Tigray had ended and that stabilising the region should now be the immediate priority. Cameroon Hudson, an analyst and consultant on African peace and security, says there are various reasons for the TPLF's rapid defeat. "The TPLF has lost popular support at home. It is fragmented, it does not possess the advanced military technology necessary to match the ENDF [Ethiopian National Defence Forces]," he says. "It has lost many of its generals, strategic thinkers, finest diplomats and fighters, either through defections or arrests. The infighting within the TPLF leadership has caused significant damage." Abraha Hailezgi, a scholar at Mekelle University, agrees. "The army lacks a clear political vision. In recent years, it has become associated with coercion, abuses, forced recruitment and arbitrary actions. As a result, many people have come to view the TPLF army as an adversary rather than a force acting on their behalf," he says. Speaking by telephone from an undisclosed location, TPLF spokesperson Mikael Asgedom denies that the group has lost. Instead, he describes it as a deliberate tactical and strategic retreat. "This is not a defeat," he tells the BBC. Reuters Dozens of people were killed in drone strikes during the short conflict He says the TPLF "intentionally allowed the ENDF to advance deeper into the heartland of Tigray", where it can be isolated and confronted on favourable terrain. "We chose not to fight on terms favourable to the enemy." The TPLF is preparing for a major counteroffensive, he says, adding that TPLF fighters have launched attacks against Ethiopian forces in several locations following their withdrawal from the region's towns, arguing that these operations demonstrated the group's continued military capability. It is hard to get verified information from Tigray and the BBC is unable to report from there. But phone lines and the internet, which were cut when fighting broke out, have now been restored. Residents in different parts of Tigray tell the BBC that fighting is continuing in central, northern and north-western parts of Tigray, with the use of heavy artillery and drone strikes. Eyewitnesses around Sheraro, a town near the Eritrean border, report heavy fighting involving artillery and ground forces in recent days. "We could hear heavy artillery fire from the Sheraro direction. People are concerned because there is no sense of security," a businessman tells the BBC on condition of anonymity. He adds that military convoys from both sides had moved towards Sheraro, while a motorcycle operator in the southern town of Yechila says military checkpoints are still active. Memories of the devastating 2020-2022 Tigray war remain raw for many residents. The conflict saw widespread human rights abuses and allegations of ethnic cleansing in Western Tigray, while estimates suggest the war claimed hundreds of thousands of lives. As soldiers from Eritrea, accused of some of the worst atrocities in the previous conflict, and Ethiopia have reappeared in Tigray's towns, many residents describe a profound sense of fear and anxiety, saying the sight of the troops has reopened still-fresh wounds. Military sources aligned with the federal army say operations against the TPLF are continuing, with recent fighting and troop movements reported in northern Tigray, near the Eritrean border, as well as across central Tigray's rugged highlands. They claim the TPLF's capabilities are being steadily degraded. Security analysts and observers agree that unrest is likely to continue for some time. "I see a situation in which there could be a prolonged war in Tigray," Yared Tibebu, a well-known Ethiopian commentator based in the US, tells the BBC. Yared argues that the TPLF has a long history of waging protracted armed struggles and believes the movement is once again preparing for a lengthy conflict. He believes that once the group has reorganised its military and political structures, it may attempt to resume offensive operations. However he believes this will not happen for some time because of internal divisions - a suggestion dismissed by TPLF spokesperson Mikael. Reuters The army says it seized all these weapons from the TPLF during the fighting Hudson rejects the idea that Tigray is heading towards a prolonged war but agrees that the region may not be truly peaceful for some time. "The TPLF may continue a low-level insurgency and guerrilla campaign, but that is not war. I do not think there will be a wider-scale conflict between the federal forces and the TPLF." He says the TPLF no longer possesses the size, strength or military capability required to effectively confront federal forces, which he says have significantly expanded and modernised in recent years. "The TPLF has also lost much of its public support and cannot easily rebuild its ranks through recruitment," he says. Yared, on the other hand, points to the TPLF's history of overcoming setbacks as evidence that the movement could recover to sustain a prolonged struggle. "The TPLF has overcome many major challenges in the past. It is wrong to conclude that it has no public support. It is a political movement with a history stretching back more than 50 years," he says. Anadolu via Getty Images Most Mekelle residents only have money for the basic necessities at the moment What Yared sees as a strength, Hudson sees as a weakness, saying the TPLF is still "trapped in the past", and continues to behave as a dominant party within Tigray, even though the situation has changed. "It is a movement that has not evolved, modernised or expanded." While Hudson argues that the TPLF is not equipped to sustain a major military campaign, the TPLF spokesman says the group obtains weapons and logistical supplies from the Ethiopian military. "We seize weapons from our enemy, and the weaponry that has entered Tigray will, sooner or later, become ours." In early October, eyewitnesses told the BBC they had seen Eritrean troops in Tigray amid reports they were backing the TPLF . However, they appear to have returned home and Hudson thinks the country would be wary of becoming further embroiled in the conflict. "First, Eritrea does not have unlimited resources. Second, the TPLF is no more an effective military force, and Eritrean leaders may have concluded that supporting it at this stage would not yield significant military gains," he says. "Third, Eritrea would have to consider the risk of provoking a confrontation with Ethiopia if it openly backs the TPLF." Sources in the Ethiopia army tell the BBC that senior members of the TPLF's political leadership were briefly based in Eritrea, however, they say the authorities ordered them to leave in early November, shortly after President Isaias Afwerki returned from Russia. According to the sources, the move was driven by concerns that Ethiopia could use their presence as a reason to invade. Hudson also argues that Eritrea's renewed diplomatic engagement with the US, whose relations with the TPLF have long been strained, could further discourage Asmara from providing meaningful support to the movement. In September, seven Ethiopian rebel groups led by the TPLF announced the formation of a new coalition called the Alliance for Survival, aimed at removing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government. Seven rebel groups from across Ethiopia have announced a new alliance Yared believes the alliance could give the TPLF the strength to keep on fighting. "Its members can combine their strengths. The TDF [the TPLF's military wing] has leadership experience and organisational capacity, while Fano [an ethnic Amhara militia] is believed to have between 70,000 and 80,000 fighters. "If conditions emerge that allow the forces to co-ordinate effectively, the TPLF's current difficulties may not last long," he says. Hudson, however, rejects that argument, insisting that the alliance is unlikely to alter the balance of power. "I don't think the TPLF can be saved by this alliance. The ethnic militias have not demonstrated the capacity, either individually or collectively, to pose a serious threat to federal forces. We should not underestimate the strength of the federal army," he says. Abraha from Mekelle University argues that the conflict in Tigray will only truly be over if the federal government addresses the region's feeling that it has been marginalised, both economically and politically by the current government. However, many Tigrayan elites and political observers remain wary of the federal government's intentions. They question whether the authorities in Addis Ababa are genuinely seeking to address Tigray's problems, or whether they are taking advantage of the region's weakness to boost their influence. In the meantime, many ordinary people in Tigray say their priority is peace. "Peace seems slow in coming. Most people are tired of politics. Whatever happens, we only want peace and a chance to rebuild our lives," says Firut from her beauty salon in Mekelle. Following a brief war that began in late September, federal forces quickly took control of Tigray's capital, Mekelle, with TPLF forces claiming a "strategic withdrawal." Despite government assertions that the conflict is over, reports indicate ongoing fighting in various regions of Tigray, including heavy artillery use. Analysts suggest the TPLF has lost popular support and military capability, but TPLF officials maintain they are regrouping for a counteroffensive. The situation remains tense, with many residents expressing fear and uncertainty about the future. While some experts predict a prolonged conflict, others believe the TPLF's diminished strength will prevent a large-scale resurgence. Ambassador Confirmation to U.S. Recognition of Somaliland November 15, 2026 5 min read WASHINGTON , U.S. Senator Ted Cruz has publicly tied his support for President Donald Trump’s nominee for ambassador to Somalia, Devin Kennington, to the State Department moving toward formal recognition of Somaliland, escalating a pressure campaign that places a confirmation vote at the center of a significant shift in U.S. foreign policy. “President Trump has made his position on Somaliland clear: Somaliland is a totally different country than Somalia,” Cruz said in a post on X on Friday. “The State Department should be taking steps in line with the President’s guidance, up to and including recognizing Somaliland’s independence.” Cruz’s public Social Media statement followed a contentious confirmation hearing on November 10 before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, where he pressed Kennington on whether he agreed with Trump’s characterization of Somaliland. According to reporting by AllAfrica and the Horn Diplomat, Kennington acknowledged that “the conditions on the ground, yes, are very different in Hargeisa and in Somaliland than they are elsewhere throughout Somalia,” but stopped short of endorsing formal recognition, instead reiterating that existing U.S. policy recognizes Somalia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. “I think President Trump is exactly right. Somaliland is not Somalia,” Cruz responded during the hearing. “The President has made his position clear, and I believe it is time for the United States to formally recognize Somaliland.” He then questioned why the State Department had not moved forward, asking, “What specifically is preventing the State Department from doing so?” Kennington, according to Breitbart, said he could not explain why the State Department had not advanced recognition or identify any specific obstacles, while expressing support for expanding U.S. engagement with Somaliland. Cruz ended the exchange by stating, “I think your confirmation depends on the State Department following the President’s guidance.” A Policy Split Within the Administration The exchange exposes a visible gap between the White House and the State Department on Somaliland policy. Trump first described Somaliland as “a totally different country” from Somalia during a rally in Ohio in October 2026, remarks that prompted celebrations in Hargeisa and were welcomed by Somaliland’s government as an acknowledgment of its distinct status. Cruz had previously endorsed that description, stating on X that it was “well past time for the United States to formally recognize it.” The State Department, however, has not shifted its formal position. Kennington’s testimony confirmed that the department continues to recognize Somalia’s sovereignty over Somaliland, even as it pursues “further engagement” with Hargeisa on commercial opportunities, Red Sea security, and its favorable position toward China. The nominee pledged to visit Somaliland if confirmed, signaling a willingness to deepen ties without altering the legal status quo. Cruz’s leverage is the confirmation process. By publicly conditioning his vote on the State Department’s policy shift, he is using the Senate’s advise-and-consent role to force a bureaucratic decision that the administration has not resolved internally. The Texas Republican had met Somaliland President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi in Washington in September, where discussions covered international recognition, security cooperation, and economic ties. Somaliland’s Strategic Pitch The push for recognition comes as Somaliland has intensified its lobbying of Washington, offering access to Berbera Port on the Gulf of Aden and potential mineral partnerships in exchange for diplomatic support. In interviews during his U.S. visit, President Abdullahi emphasized Somaliland’s role in regional security and its willingness to host American military assets. The strategy mirrors the approach that secured Israel’s recognition in December 2025, a precedent Cruz cited repeatedly during the hearing. The Somaliland community in Minnesota has publicly thanked Cruz for his advocacy, urging the administration to take “meaningful steps towards formal recognition.” Critical Note Ted Cruz’s intervention is a significant escalation, but it is not a policy change. The senator has used the confirmation of a mid-level ambassador to force a debate that the State Department has been content to avoid. Whether that pressure succeeds depends on whether the White House is prepared to override its own diplomatic bureaucracy, and whether Kennington is willing to risk his confirmation to preserve the status quo. The stakes for Somalia are substantial. If the United States moves toward recognition, it would break with the African Union’s consensus, undermine the federal government’s claim to territorial integrity, and align Washington with Israel’s controversial precedent. Mogadishu has consistently rejected any recognition of Somaliland, and a U.S. shift would be a diplomatic defeat of the first order for President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s government, already facing a constitutional crisis at home. For Somaliland, Cruz’s campaign is the most serious opening it has had in Washington. But the gap between a senator’s advocacy and a president’s signature is wide. Trump’s rhetorical support has not yet translated into formal action, and the State Department’s resistance suggests that the institutional weight of the U.S. government remains on the side of the status quo. Cruz has forced the issue into the open. He has not resolved it. The two sides signed a Memorandum of Understanding on consultations between the two foreign ministries, establishing a structured mechanism for regular reviews of bilateral relations. According to the Indian Ministry of External Affairs, the discussions covered trade, medical cooperation, education, and capacity-building, alongside an exchange of views on recent geopolitical developments in the region. Ranganathan also met Defence Minister Ahmed Moallim Fiqi, with talks focused on strengthening defence cooperation, particularly in maritime security, counter-terrorism, and capacity-building, as well as the evolving regional security environment. A Relationship Being Rebuilt The consultations formalise a relationship that has been gradually re-energised over the past year. India closed its resident mission in Mogadishu in 1991 after the outbreak of the civil war, and for decades engaged with Somalia through its High Commission in Nairobi, which is concurrently accredited to Mogadishu. That arrangement has now been supplemented by a structured bilateral dialogue. The groundwork was laid in April 2026, when Somalia’s Foreign Minister Abdisalam Abdi Ali formally accepted the credentials of India’s newly appointed Ambassador to Somalia, Dr. Adarsh Swaika, who operates from Nairobi. The two sides pledged to convert diplomatic goodwill into concrete economic projects, as detailed in the coverage of the credential ceremony . President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud formally received Swaika’s credentials at Villa Somalia in August 2026. The diplomatic momentum had been building since late 2025. In October, Somalia’s Ambassador to Kenya hosted Swaika in Nairobi for talks on trade, education, healthcare, and institutional capacity building, as reported in the coverage of the Nairobi talks . In January 2026, Foreign Minister Abdisalam travelled to New Delhi for the Arab-India Foreign Ministers’ Meeting, where he met his Indian counterpart S. Jaishankar to discuss trade, capacity building, and multilateral engagement, as detailed in the coverage of the New Delhi visit . Trade between the two countries stood at approximately $800 million in the 2024-25 fiscal year, overwhelmingly weighted toward Indian exports of cereals, sugar, vehicles, machinery, and plastics. Somalia’s exports to India, by contrast, were valued at just over $35 million, consisting mainly of iron and steel, oil seeds, and raw hides. The Sovereignty Dimension India has also positioned itself as a supporter of Somalia’s territorial integrity. In January 2026, New Delhi formally opposed Israel’s recognition of Somaliland, with the Ministry of External Affairs stating that it reaffirmed “the importance of respecting the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Federal Republic of Somalia,” as reported in the coverage of India’s statement . That position aligns New Delhi with Mogadishu on one of Somalia’s most sensitive diplomatic issues. The defence discussions add a strategic layer to a relationship that has historically been commercial and developmental. India has long been a maritime security actor in the western Indian Ocean, and its naval deployments have been central to the fight against Somali piracy. The meeting between Ranganathan and Fiqi suggests that New Delhi is prepared to deepen that cooperation, potentially including capacity-building for Somali maritime forces. Critical Note The first Somalia-India Foreign Office Consultations are a welcome development, but they should be read for what they are: a formalisation of a relationship that has been managed from a distance for over three decades. The MoU on consultations provides a mechanism, not a commitment. The discussions on trade, medical cooperation, and education are necessary, but they do not yet represent a substantial shift in India’s engagement with Somalia. The defence talks are more significant. India is one of the few countries with the naval capacity and the strategic interest to contribute to maritime security in the Horn of Africa. If the consultations lead to concrete cooperation on maritime domain awareness, counter-piracy, or capacity-building for the Somali Navy, that would be a meaningful contribution. If they remain exploratory, they will be another in a long list of diplomatic engagements that produced communiqués rather than capabilities. For Somalia, the relationship with India is part of a broader diversification strategy. Mogadishu has cultivated ties with Türkiye, Egypt, the UAE, Qatar, and Algeria. India adds a major Asian power to that list, one with its own interests in the Indian Ocean and its own concerns about Chinese influence in the region. The consultations are a start. Whether they produce results will depend on whether both sides are prepared to move from dialogue to investment. (Reuters Photo) Mogadishu (HOL) — Türkiye's Ministry of National Defence has denied reports that it plans to deploy 15,000 troops to Somalia at the request of the federal government, reaffirming its commitment to military training and counterterrorism cooperation with Mogadishu. Speaking at a news briefing Thursday, ministry spokesperson Rear Adm. Zeki Aktürk rejected claims circulating in Turkish and Somali media about a large-scale deployment of Turkish forces to Somalia. “Claims that Türkiye will send 15,000 troops to Somalia at the request of the Somali government do not reflect the truth,” the ministry said. advertisements Aktürk confirmed that Türkiye already maintains a military presence in Somalia through the Somali-Turkish Task Force and an air component command. He said Turkish forces would continue supporting Somalia's counterterrorism capabilities through military assistance, training and advisory services. The denial follows reports suggesting that Somalia had sought additional military assistance from international partners, including Türkiye, amid concerns about security as African Union troop-contributing countries prepare to withdraw some of their forces. Some reports also alleged that fighters from Syrian armed groups involved in the overthrow of the former Syrian government could be deployed to Somalia. Those claims have not been substantiated. Türkiye operates the TURKSOM military training facility in Mogadishu, where Turkish instructors have trained Somali military personnel as part of efforts to strengthen the Somali National Army. adinsideThe facility, which opened in 2017, has played a significant role in developing Somalia's military capabilities, including training specialized units involved in operations against al-Shabab. The Turkish statement comes days after Turkish Ambassador to Somalia Ferhat Alkan met Somali National Security Adviser Aweys Haji Yusuf Ahmed in Mogadishu to discuss military cooperation, counterterrorism operations and regional security developments. During Tuesday's meeting, the two officials reviewed Somalia's security situation and efforts to strengthen cooperation between the countries as African Union forces prepare for changes to their deployments. “Türkiye continues to contribute to the peace, stability and security of Somalia, as it has in the past,” the Turkish Embassy said following the meeting. According to Somalia's Office of the National Security Adviser, the discussions also covered political developments, operations against al-Shabab and broader bilateral cooperation. The office said Somalia appreciated Türkiye's longstanding support and emphasized the importance of continued coordination to strengthen national security. The discussions come amid uncertainty over the future of the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), particularly following Uganda's announcement that it would withdraw troops deployed under bilateral arrangements and gradually end its participation in the mission. Uganda has been one of the largest contributors to African Union military operations in Somalia since 2007, playing a major role in securing Mogadishu and supporting operations against al-Shabab. The withdrawal plans have raised concerns about the readiness of Somali forces to assume responsibility for areas previously secured by foreign troops. Somalia and Türkiye maintain a longstanding defense partnership covering military training, counterterrorism, maritime security and military capacity-building. Despite rejecting reports of an additional 15,000 troops, Ankara reaffirmed that its existing military mission would continue supporting Somalia's efforts to strengthen its armed forces and combat militant groups. The statement was issued by Somalia, Djibouti, Egypt, Qatar, Sudan, Libya, Palestine, Oman, Saudi Arabia, Mauritania, Jordan, the United Arab Emirates, Türkiye, Pakistan, Indonesia, Algeria, Kuwait and Lebanon. The countries expressed concern over what they described as Israeli restrictions on humanitarian assistance, including the entry of tents, mobile homes, shelter materials and medical supplies. Abdi Ali Barkad It is time to speak frankly. Many former Ex-Italian-Somali (South-Somalia) intellectuals, academics, and politicians appear to be preoccupied with the political affairs of the Republic of Somaliland, while conveniently overlooking the enormous challenges confronting their own country. They continue to knock on the wrong door, investing their intellectual energy and political resources in a matter that requires neither their permission nor their approval. Let us remind them of a fundamental political reality The people of Somaliland made their decision not to remain in the union with Southern Somalia . In 1991, Somaliland restored its independence following the collapse of the Somali Republic, which had been established in 1960. That political union came to an end, and Somaliland embarked on its own political journey. Whether some people accept this reality or not does not change the historical and political position of Somaliland. After 35 years, it is reasonable to ask the intellectuals and politicians of former Italian Somalia a fundamental question: For more than three decades, your country has struggled to establish effective national institutions, lasting political stability, and a functioning system of governance. The federal arrangement you adopted has not delivered the peace, unity, and institutional stability that the Somali people were promised. Political confrontations between Villa Somalia and Federal Member States continue. Armed conflicts persist in different parts of the country. National institutions remain fragile, and the security sector continues to face serious questions concerning its independence, inclusiveness, and national representation. There are also serious allegations concerning the mismanagement and disposal of public assets and the weakening of state institutions under successive administrations, particularly the current leadership. These are not minor political disagreements. They are fundamental questions about the survival, credibility, and future of your state. Now, compare this with Somaliland. Over the same period, Somaliland has developed its own political institutions, conducted six presidential elections, and elected four presidents through direct universal suffrage under a multiparty democratic system. This achievement deserves serious political and academic examination, regardless of one’s position on Somaliland’s international recognition. What is particularly difficult to understand is why intellectuals, academics, and experienced politicians continue to spend so much time debating Somaliland’s internal affairs while their own political house remains in such disarray. Where is that same intellectual energy when it comes to rebuilding national institutions? Where is the same political determination when federal authorities are in conflict with one another? Where is the same academic scrutiny when questions arise about public resources, national security, corruption, and the accountability of those governing your country? Why is Somaliland constantly on your political agenda when the most urgent national problems are at your own doorstep? An intellectual’s responsibility is to confront reality, not escape from it. A politician’s duty is to serve the people, not to distract them from the failures of governance. We respectfully but firmly advise you to redirect your attention towards the internal affairs of your own country. Concentrate on building a functioning federal system. Establish genuine national institutions. Create an inclusive and professional national army. Resolve political disputes between federal and regional authorities. Protect public assets. Fight corruption. Restore public confidence in government and give your people a reason to believe in their country’s future. These are the responsibilities that demand your experience, knowledge, and political leadership. Somaliland is not responsible for the political failures of your country, and its people should not be expected to put their political future on hold because others have failed to resolve their own problems. You cannot build a nation by constantly questioning the political choices of your neighbors. You cannot establish credible leadership while ignoring failures within your own administration. And you cannot lecture others about statehood when your own state-building project remains unfinished. My message is neither an invitation to hostility nor a rejection of dialogue. It is a call for political maturity, intellectual honesty, and respect for the choices of peoples. Respect Somaliland’s political journey. Accept that its people have their own political aspirations and priorities. Stop treating Somaliland as a permanent subject of political obsession. You have a country that needs your attention, a population that needs effective leadership, institutions that need rebuilding, and a political system that urgently needs reform. Put your own house in order. Rebuild your nation. Resolve your internal divisions. Establish credible institutions. And when you have made meaningful progress in those responsibilities, we can sit down and discuss matters of mutual interest as neighbours. Until then, stop knocking on Somaliland’s door. Your own house is the one that needs urgent attention. Respect political realities. Respect the people’s choices. Build your own nation first. According to a report by Insidesomalia.net, the discussions also covered improving equipment, professional development, and the exchange of expertise to further strengthen the longstanding ties between Somalia and Türkiye. The Turkish Police Special Operations Department has played a key role in training and equipping the Haramcad unit, one of the best-trained and best-equipped specialised units within the Somali Police Force. The Haramcad Model and Its Limits The Haramcad unit is not a conventional police force. It is a specialized commando unit that has been at the center of Türkiye’s security assistance to Somalia, alongside the Gorgor military commandos. More than 1,000 specialized personnel within the Somali Police Force, including Haramcad members, have been trained by Türkiye, according to Ambassador Alper Aktaş. The Turkish Embassy in Mogadishu has described the training as continuing “uninterrupted,” and Ambassador Ferhat Alkan visited the Somali Police Force headquarters in October to reaffirm Ankara’s commitment to the unit, as detailed in the coverage of the ambassador’s visit . But the unit’s effectiveness depends on more than training and equipment. It depends on integration into a broader security architecture that includes the police, the military, and the justice system. A well-trained commando unit operating without accountability mechanisms or a functioning criminal justice system is a tool that can protect civilians or intimidate them, depending on who is giving the orders. The Haramcad has been deployed in operations against Al-Shabaab , including a battle in Basra, about 18 miles from Mogadishu, in August 2026. The unit fought there for over a week alongside the army, but by September 9, government troops had withdrawn toward Dayniile, leaving Al-Shabaab to take ground along the Afgooye road without a fight, according to local sources cited by the Middle East Forum. That outcome suggests that even well-trained units cannot compensate for broader strategic and political failures. A Partnership Under Political Pressure Türkiye’s security relationship with Somalia has come under increasing scrutiny as the political crisis in Mogadishu has deepened. Critics of President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud view Ankara as too closely aligned with his administration, particularly as disputes over elections, federal authority, and the leadership of South West State have escalated into armed confrontation. The most serious allegations concern reported Turkish air operations and the use of Turkish-supplied military equipment during the conflict in South West State. Local officials and forces aligned with former regional president Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed Laftagareen have accused Türkiye of supporting federal operations and contributing to attacks that allegedly harmed civilians. These claims have not all been independently verified, and Türkiye’s government has rejected allegations that its military presence is intended to interfere in Somalia’s internal political affairs. The distinction between supporting Somalia’s national security and supporting the political agenda of the incumbent administration is fundamental. A military partnership intended to strengthen Somalia should not become associated with a domestic political struggle over who governs the country’s regions. Critical Note Türkiye’s training of the Haramcad unit has produced a force that is better equipped and better trained than most of Somalia’s security institutions. That is a real achievement, and it deserves recognition. But the partnership is not without risks. The Haramcad unit operates in a political environment where the line between security operations and political repression is not always clear. The unit’s deployment in South West State, and the allegations of civilian harm that accompanied it, have damaged Türkiye’s reputation among some Somali communities. Ankara’s silence on those allegations, and its blanket denial of interference, have done little to reassure critics. For Somalia, the Haramcad model offers a template for building capable, professional forces. But a unit that is trained and equipped by a foreign partner, and that operates in the most sensitive security spaces, needs to be accountable to the public it serves, not just to the government of the day. The training and equipment are necessary. They are not sufficient. The question is whether the partnership is building a police force that serves the public, or one that serves the political interests of the incumbent administration. football.summary: أعلنت لجنة الاستئناف بالاتحاد السوداني لكرة القدم قرارًا مفاجئًا بشأن لقب الدوري السوداني، حيث ألغت قرارها السابق الذي منح اللقب لنادي المريخ، وأعادت اللقب لنادي الهلال. جاء هذا القرار بعد قبول طلب المراجعة المقدم من الهلال، الذي أكد استحقاقه للقب بعد فوزه على المريخ في المباراة الأخيرة من الموسم الماضي. وأوضحت اللجنة أنها عقدت اجتماعين في 9 و10 نوفمبر، حيث استندت إلى تقرير الحكم في المباراة. وأصدر نادي الهلال بيانًا رسميًا يعلن فيه استرداده للقب، مؤكدًا مكانته كأكثر الأندية تتويجًا بالبطولات في السودان. يذكر أن الموسم الماضي شهد جدلًا كبيرًا حول قانونية مشاركة بعض لاعبي الهلال، مما أدى إلى منح اللقب للمريخ بعد استئناف. هذا القرار يعيد الأمور إلى نصابها ويؤكد تفوق الهلال في الساحة الرياضية السودانية.
